- Daoist Philosophy: Social Critique | Zhuangzi’s Butcher Ding: Kind: captions Language: en Butcher Ding: A Slaughter Ballet Ding, the butcher, slaughtered an ox for&nbsp;Wen-Hui, the ruler. He tore it with his hands,&nbsp;shoved it with his shoulders, whacked it&nbsp;with his feet, and hit it with his knees.&nbsp;&nbsp; The smacking and the crushing, the knife’s&nbsp;hissing and slicing: all were perfectly in tune.&nbsp;&nbsp; Motions were in time with the “Mulberry Grove”&nbsp;dance, and sounds matched the Jingshou music.&nbsp; Wen-Hui, the ruler, said: “Magnificent!&nbsp; How can skill reach such perfection?”&nbsp; Stowing his knife, the butcher&nbsp;said: “What I care about is the Dao,&nbsp;&nbsp; so I go a step further than skill. When I began&nbsp;slaughtering oxen, all I would see was oxen; but after three years, I wouldn’t&nbsp;even see a whole ox anymore. These days, I approach them with the spirit,&nbsp;not looking at them with my eyes. My sense&nbsp;perception stops and my spiritual determination goes to work. I rely on the natural structures&nbsp;to strike through the big cracks, lead through&nbsp;the big holes, follow through as it must be.&nbsp;&nbsp; I never cut through the thicker nodes and sinews,&nbsp; and of course not through the big bones. Decent&nbsp;butchers change their knives yearly. They slash.&nbsp; Average butchers change their knives monthly.&nbsp;They hack. I’ve got my knife for nineteen years&nbsp;now and slaughtered thousands of oxen with it.&nbsp;&nbsp; Its blade is just as good as a new one right off&nbsp;the whetstone. Those joints have space in between, and a knife’s blade has no thickness. When&nbsp;what has no thickness goes into the in-between,&nbsp;&nbsp; there is surely more than enough room for the&nbsp;blade to ramble around at ease. This is why&nbsp;after nineteen years my knife’s blade is just&nbsp; as good as a new one right off the whetstone.&nbsp;&nbsp; Still, each time I encounter some gristle that I see&nbsp; is hard to handle, I hold back most cautiously.&nbsp;&nbsp; My eyes fixed on that spot, I almost grind down&nbsp;to a halt. Then I move the knife subtly, and in&nbsp;an instant the butchering has been done: the pieces&nbsp;lie on the ground like scattered soil. Presenting&nbsp;my knife, I stand, turning to face all four&nbsp;directions, with an air of pride and satisfaction.&nbsp;&nbsp; Then I wipe the knife clean and put it away.” Wen-Hui, the ruler, said: “Splendid! I hear the words of Ding, the butcher,&nbsp;and understand how to nourish one’s life!” This story of a ritual slaughter may be&nbsp;regarded as more or less the mother&nbsp;&nbsp; of all the so-called Daoist “knack stories” that&nbsp;have attracted much attention throughout the ages.&nbsp;&nbsp; These stories typically describe peculiar artisans&nbsp;enacting their craft with miraculous skill.&nbsp;&nbsp; They are usually taken to be, if somewhat&nbsp;exaggerated, Daoist role model stories intended&nbsp;&nbsp; to illustrate the incredible performance&nbsp;capacities resulting from Daoist exercise.&nbsp;&nbsp; Determined dedication to a Daoist&nbsp;cultivation regime of body and mind,&nbsp;&nbsp; it is suggested, will extraordinarily enhance&nbsp;one’s physical and spiritual potentials.&nbsp; Butcher Ding’s explanation of his sublime&nbsp;slaughter makes ample use of major Daoist themes&nbsp;and concepts. Right away he points out that he’s a&nbsp;man of the Dao, and not just a regular craftsman.&nbsp;&nbsp; He claims some higher aspiration&nbsp;beyond mundane professional expertise.&nbsp;&nbsp; In an almost meditative state, he no longer&nbsp;relies on his senses. This state is described&nbsp;similarly to a line from the Daodejing as a&nbsp;kind of seeing without looking (視之不見). The&nbsp;butcher then speaks of his motions with Daoist&nbsp;imagery as a spontaneous and effortless flow,&nbsp;&nbsp; seeking out empty spaces and exerting&nbsp;strength without using force.&nbsp;&nbsp; Such avoidance of friction allows his knife to&nbsp;maintain its immaculate sharpness— symbolizing the&nbsp;pristine vitality that Daoist practitioners&nbsp;are supposed to preserve. What is more,&nbsp;in all its durability, the knife operates in&nbsp;the mode of “rambling around at ease”, or you 遊:&nbsp;&nbsp; the central notion of well-being in the Zhuangzi. The butcher’s self-depiction as a Daoist master&nbsp;is emphatically confirmed by Lord Wen-Hui&nbsp;at the end of the story. He credits Ding for&nbsp;making him understand the art of yang sheng&nbsp;養生, of “nourishing life”. &nbsp; This expression&nbsp;not only provided the chapter in the Zhuangzi in&nbsp;which the story occurs with its title, but became&nbsp;an emblematic term for the cultivation of vitality&nbsp; in Chinese culture. No wonder then, that the story&nbsp;has been read as an iconic representation&nbsp;of Daoist practice. Such a reading, however,&nbsp;disregards the many incongruities woven into the&nbsp;text. Once these incongruities are taken note of,&nbsp;under the surface of a Daoist role model tale,&nbsp;a darkly humorous social critique emerges.&nbsp; Sacrificial rituals involving the slaughter&nbsp;of animals were a common event at the courts&nbsp;of early Chinese rulers: they adorned their rule&nbsp;with a religious aura, manifested their power and&nbsp;wealth and aestheticized it; and also provided an&nbsp;occasion for lavish banquets and feasts creating a&nbsp;bond between rulers and their feudal cliques. The&nbsp;Zhuangzi’s story of Ding, the butcher, however,&nbsp;&nbsp; grossly violates the standard etiquette&nbsp;of such rituals: As is mentioned in the&nbsp;first chapter of the Zhuangzi, the roles of ritual&nbsp;performers were strictly separated from butchers and cooks The Butcher Ding&nbsp;story breaks this taboo and puts the gruesome kill&nbsp;right in front of the eyes of the ruler—&nbsp;&nbsp; and of the readers of the story. As if in a Quentin Tarantino&nbsp;movie, a gory and unreal slaughter ballet unfolds. Quite shockingly, the beautiful artistic&nbsp;performances at the heart of a ritual banquet&nbsp;&nbsp; take on the form of the dismemberment&nbsp;of a huge living animal.&nbsp;&nbsp; The visual and emotional horrors of&nbsp;slicing up a body, splitting it apart,&nbsp;&nbsp; and splattering its blood, bizarrely&nbsp;blend with refined music and dance.&nbsp; The ritual slaughter of an ox is also the theme&nbsp;of another quite famous story about Zhuang Zhou.&nbsp;&nbsp; Here, Zhuang Zhou explains his refusal to take on&nbsp;a government job by comparing political officials&nbsp;&nbsp; with sacrificial oxen at court: They may be&nbsp;taken care of nicely for a time, but only to&nbsp;eventually get slaughtered. The message of this&nbsp;story blatantly contradicts the story of Ding,&nbsp;the butcher, who ceremoniously kills the oxen&nbsp;Zhuang Zhou himself desired never to become.&nbsp; Ding, the butcher, was a legendary figure&nbsp;in early China, also known from other texts&nbsp;as a model of skill. However, just as with&nbsp;the equally legendary horse trainer Bo Le 伯樂,&nbsp;&nbsp; the Zhuangzi reverses the common evaluation of&nbsp;these figures. Rather than positive models of&nbsp;humans making good use of animals, they appear&nbsp;as destructive characters who violently kill&nbsp;or domesticate animals against their will. The&nbsp;butcher’s long-term practice of his art has,&nbsp;ironically, “spiritually elevated” him to&nbsp;a level where he isn’t even able to see an&nbsp;ox as a living being anymore. He has become all&nbsp;but blind for the life and suffering of others. And yet, Ding, the butcher, undoubtedly has&nbsp;marvellous capabilities and describes himself&nbsp;as a Daoist virtuoso. The very fact, though, that&nbsp;he speaks in such a self-aggrandizing manner, his&nbsp;“air of pride and satisfaction,” and his arrogant&nbsp;claim to be “a man of the Dao” sets him apart from&nbsp;most other protagonists of knack stories in the&nbsp;Zhuangzi who are typically reluctant to speak.&nbsp; Ding, the butcher is an incongruent,&nbsp;satirically inverted Daoist master.&nbsp;&nbsp; He does not shun public office, but&nbsp;delights in being a ruler’s slaughterer.&nbsp;&nbsp; Instead of avoiding the sphere of political ritual&nbsp;with its artifice and excess, he is at the center&nbsp;of it. Instead of being cautious with words,&nbsp;he boasts about his skills. Most incongruously,&nbsp;he teaches a ruler the art of “nourishing life” by means of a brutal killing.&nbsp;&nbsp; And the incongruous main symbol of&nbsp;this supposed art of nourishing life,&nbsp;&nbsp; highlighted throughout the story, and then&nbsp;at the end proudly presented to all sides,&nbsp;&nbsp; wiped clean of blood, and cautiously stored&nbsp;to be used again for the next slaughter with&nbsp;all its sharpness intact—is a butcher’s knife. Once the grotesque incongruities of the story&nbsp;are taken into account, Ding, the butcher, no&nbsp;longer appears as a Daoist virtuoso, but as a&nbsp;Daoist sell-out. He put himself in the service of&nbsp;the rulers of his time—which, for good reason, is&nbsp;labelled the “Warring States” period. Innumerable&nbsp;rulers fought constantly against one another,&nbsp;striving for power and wealth. Regular people&nbsp;were conscripted into armies or for large building projects; punishments were frequent and harsh, and&nbsp;food shortages were no rarity. Rulers, however,&nbsp;often managed to nourish their own lives well&nbsp;by waging war—the devastating effects of which&nbsp;early Daoist texts often lament. The symbol of&nbsp;the knife in butcher Ding’s hand can be taken to&nbsp;represent the endless slaughter and suffering&nbsp;inflicted by rulers of the time on their people.&nbsp;&nbsp; Like that knife, the rulers’ warfare&nbsp;seemed never to lose its efficiency&nbsp;and produced an endless supply of fresh dead meat.&nbsp; At the same time elaborate rituals provided an&nbsp;ornamental framework supplying the ruling class&nbsp;with aesthetic splendour and spiritual elevation,&nbsp;&nbsp; allowing them to feel perfectly “at ease”&nbsp;in the midst of the horror they created.

- A Cook Never Dulled His Blade in 18 Years - Zhuangzi on Following the Grain of the World: Kind: captions Language: en There is a cook in the Zhuangzi who cuts an ox not with effort, not with the grunting, mechanical, blade-against-bone labor that butchering requires. He moves through the animal the way a musician moves through a piece of music with the specific, fluid, warm, completely unhurried quality of someone who is not working against anything because they have found the places where there is nothing to work against. His cleaver never dulls. In 18 years of cutting, the blade has not once touched bone or gristle. He does not see the ox as a full animal and hack his way through it. He sees the natural structure, the spaces between the joints, the cavities where the tissue separates cleanly, and follows the grain of the thing rather than forcing his way through it. His lord watches and says, "Your skill is excellent." The cook puts down his cleaver, says, "What I follow is the Tao, something beyond mere skill. I work with my mind and not with my eye. My mind works without the control of the senses. I glide through the large cavities where they exist. I do not touch the ligaments or tendons. A good cook changes his chopper once a year because he cuts. An ordinary cook once a month because he hacks. He does not cut. He does not hack. He finds the space where the cutting is not necessary, where the thing yields not because force was applied, but because the mover has learned to feel where the thing wants to open." This is the philosophy of Zhuangzi, and it is the strangest, the funniest, the most difficult, and the most practically useful philosophical tradition in the history of human thought. We live inside a philosophy of effort. The culture's primary story about achievement is this: You identify the goal, you assess the gap between where you are and where you want to be, you apply sustained effort to close the gap, you monitor your progress, you adjust your strategy, you persist through the resistance, and you arrive through will, through discipline, through the accumulation of deliberate, directed, continuous force applied in the right direction. This is not wrong. Effort is real and necessary, and there is work in the world that requires exactly this approach. The Zhuangzi is not a philosophy of laziness or of the passive acceptance of whatever happens to arrive. But Zhuangzi looked at this story, the story of the self forcing its way through the world by will and method and the relentless application of strategic intention, and noticed something in it that the story itself could not see from the inside. The force is the problem. Not always, not for everything, but for the deepest kind of work, the work that is not the assembly of parts according to a blueprint, but the following of something alive, something moving, something that has its own grain and its own direction and its own slow, deliberate, natural openings. Force closes the very spaces skill is trying to find. The cook who hacks touches bone. The cook who follows the Tao glides through the cavities that force would never find. Zhuangzi, his actual name was Zhuang Zhou, lived in the 4th century BC in the state of Song in what is now Henan province in central China. He was a contemporary of Mencius, who was developing the Confucian tradition, and he spent a significant portion of his writing arguing with that tradition. Not bitterly, but with the specific, delighted, completely unembarrassed humor of a man who found the contrast between official Confucian earnestness and the actual texture of human experience genuinely funny. He was offered a position of high government office and declined. The story the tradition tells is that a royal messenger came to find him while he was fishing, and Zhuangzi, without looking up from the water, said that he had heard there was a sacred tortoise in the capital that had been dead for 3,000 years and was kept in a place of honor, wrapped in silk. He asked whether the tortoise would prefer to be dead and honored or alive and dragging its tail in the mud. The messenger said, "Alive, dragging its tail in the mud." Zhuangzi said, "Go away. I, too, will drag my tail in the mud." He wanted the mud. He wanted the living thing in its natural element, not preserved, not honored, not wrapped in the silk of official recognition. Alive, dirty, present in the actual texture of the actual world. This preference for the alive and muddy over the dead and honored is the whole of his philosophy in one story. The Zhuangzi, the text that bears his name, compiled across generations, containing material from many hands, but animated throughout by a single, unmistakable voice, is the most difficult and the most rewarding philosophical text in the Chinese tradition, it is not organized like a philosophical treatise, does not proceed from premises to arguments to conclusions. It moves the way the cook moves through the ox, through stories and parables and jokes and sudden unexpected turns that leave you somewhere you did not expect to be. There is a woodworker who carves a bell stand so beautiful that people think a spirit must have guided his hands. He says, "I fasted until my mind was one. My skill was concentrated. My selfhood dissolved. I entered the forest and looked at the trees until I found the one that had already, in its natural form, become the bell stand. Then I brought my hand to the work." He did not impose the form. He found it. The bell stand was already in the tree, already present in the natural structure of what was there, and his skill consisted of finding it, rather than forcing it into a shape the tree had not already prepared. This is what Zhuangzi means by following the Tao in practice, not passivity. The woodworker is enormously skilled, has spent decades developing his craft. But skill in the Zhuangzi understanding is not the ability to impose. It is the ability to receive, to be sensitive enough to the grain of the thing to find where it wants to go. I want to stay with the butterfly because it is the most famous passage in the Zhuangzi and the one that most people know and the one that is most consistently reduced to a pretty thought when it is actually a structural argument about the nature of reality. Zhuangzi writes, "Once upon a time, I, Zhuangzi, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering hither and thither, to all intents and purposes, a butterfly. I was conscious only of my happiness as a butterfly, unaware that I was Zhuangzi. Soon, I awoke, and there lay Zhuangzi, fast asleep. But then I wondered, was I Zhuangzi dreaming of being a butterfly, or am I now a butterfly dreaming of being Zhuangzi?" This is not a question about whether reality is real. It is a question about the solidity of the boundaries we draw between things, between sleeping and waking, between the dreaming self and the waking self, between Zhuangzi the man and the butterfly in the dream, between the categories that the mind uses to organize experience and the experience itself, which flows continuously, refusing the neat divisions that language and thought impose on it. The Zhuangzi calls the space between these categories a necessary transition, the hinge point, the place where one perspective becomes another, where what seemed fixed reveals itself to be in motion. And he says, "The person who has found this hinge, who lives at the place where the categories meet and dissolve, is the person who can move through the world finding the natural openings, following the grain, never dulling the blade because the blade is never forced against anything solid." There is a concept in the Zhuangzi, the concept that the text was built to transmit, that we have encountered before in this series, but that Zhuangzi takes further than any other philosopher in the tradition. Wu wei, effortless action, the doing that does not announce itself as doing, the work that follows the grain of the thing so precisely that no force is wasted, no resistance encountered, the task accomplished as naturally and as inevitably as water finding its level. But Zhuangzi adds something to wu wei that the Tao Te Ching does not quite say. He adds the dimension of joy. The cook does not merely perform his task without effort. He is fully present to it, takes pleasure in it, the genuine, unreserved, completely natural pleasure of a person doing the thing they were made to do in the way it wants to be done, in contact with the Tao rather than working against it. He says, "I work in accordance with my natural constitution. I slide through such great joints or cavities as there may be, according to the natural constitution of the animal. I do not even touch the convolutions of muscle and tendon, still less attempt to cut through large bones, according to the natural constitution of the animal." And implicitly, according to the natural constitution of the cook. The work that arises from the alignment of what the mover is and what the thing moved requires. This is what Zhuangzi means by skill. This is what he means by following the Tao. Not technique applied to matter. Awareness in contact with the grain of what is. Now, the bridge. Because Zhuangzi was writing in 4th century BC China, and most of us are not butchering oxen or carving bell stands, but most of us know, from the inside, the difference between the work that feels like hacking and the work that feels like finding the natural opening. Between the conversation that forces its way to a conclusion and the conversation that arrives there because the space opened. Between the creative project that comes from imposing a predetermined form and the one that reveals its own form, if you can be quiet enough and sensitive enough to see what is already there. And most of us know the exhaustion of the hacking, the blade that dulls, the effort that produces resistance that produces more effort, the experience of being in the work, but not with the work, of applying force rather than following the grain of a thing that, if you could find it, would open by itself. Zhuangzi does not have a method for finding the grain. He is suspicious of methods. The person with a method is the person who has already decided how the thing should go and has therefore stopped being sensitive to how it actually wants to go. What he offers is something prior to method, a quality of attention, the attention of the cook who has spent 18 years learning to feel the spaces, who has dissolved the self-consciousness of the person demonstrating skill and arrived at the transparency of the person simply doing the thing. Here is what Zhuangzi asks of you, practically, today. First, find where you are hacking. There is something in your work or in a relationship, or in the way you are moving through a current difficulty, where the blade is dulling, where the effort is producing resistance rather than progress, where the approach has the quality of force being applied to something that has not yielded to force and is not going to. Identify it. Not to judge the effort. The hacking is honest. The hacking is sometimes the only thing available. But to see it clearly, to ask, "Is this the right tool for this material? Is there a space here that I am cutting across rather than following?" The cook does not hack, but the cook spent years learning to feel the difference between the joint in the bone. Second, fast the mind. The woodworker who carves the bell stand says he fasted until his mind was one, not the body, the mind, until the noise of preference and judgement and the constant self-monitoring of the person who is performing competence had quieted enough for the natural structure of the thing to become visible. Once this week, before a piece of work that matters, before a conversation that matters, sit for 5 minutes with the intention of fasting the mind, not emptying it, quieting the part that is already composing the argument, already monitoring how the work is going, already measuring the progress against the predetermined outcome. Let that quiet. And then, enter the work and see whether the thing has a grain that the noise was preventing you from feeling. Third, follow something for 1 hour without a destination. Zhuangzi walked in the forests, fished in the rivers, declined the official positions, and kept the contact with the actual living, completely ungovernable texture of the world that institutional life tends to replace with its abstracted version. Once this week, 1 hour without a destination, without a productivity justification, follow something. A walk with no route, a piece of music all the way through with no other task, a conversation that is allowed to go wherever it actually wants to go. Not to achieve anything, to practice the quality of movement that follows rather than forces, that is present enough to feel the grain, that is not imposing a predetermined shape on the hour it is moving through. Notice where it goes. It will go somewhere you did not plan. Fourth, sit with the butterfly question. Not philosophically, as a direct investigation in the spirit of the forest philosophers, Zhuangzi and the Upanishads both, because they are pointing at the same territory from different directions. Once today, for 1 minute, hold the butterfly question genuinely, not as a riddle to be solved, as an opening. The boundary between the one who is reading this and the one who is dreaming last night. - TAOISM | The Philosophy Of Flow: Kind: captions Language: en That which offers no resistance, overcomes the hardest substances. That which offers no resistance can enter where there is no space. Few in the world can comprehend the teaching without words, or understand the value of non-action. Lao Tzu There’s no proof that he truly ever lived, but if he did, it should have been somewhere around the 5th and 6th century B.C, which makes him a contemporary of Confucius. Nevertheless, the Chinese philosopher Lao Tzu wrote a masterpiece called the Tao Te Ching, which is the main work of Taoism. A well-known concept that has emerged from Taoist philosophy is wu wei, that can be translated as “non-action”, “effortless action”, or the paradoxical “action of non-action”. In a practical sense, we can describe wu wei as the state of flow, often referred to as the ‘the zone’ by athletes. When athletes are in the zone, they engage in action without striving, and move through time and space almost effortlessly. There are no extremes, no worries, no ruminations; everything seems to flow in a natural course. As an introduction to the beautiful tradition of Taoism, I’d like to present you, the... ..Philosophy of Flow. The Tao Te Ching is a mysterious piece of art. Not only there’s no consensus when exactly it was written, but the existence of its author remains disputed. Nevertheless, one thing is certain: the profundity of this work has left its mark on humanity to this day. Not to mention that the Tao Te Ching is the most translated work in world literature after the Bible. The essence of Taoist philosophy is living in harmony with the Tao, also called the Way. So, what is the Tao? That’s a question we can’t really answer, and it’s futile to try. Our understanding of the Tao only goes as far as the limitations of our perception. What the Tao really is and what it looks, feels, smells or sounds like remains a mystery. Moreover, the Tao that we speak of isn’t the real Tao, according to Lao Tzu. Hence, the famous opening of the Tao Te Ching goes like this: The tao that can be described is not the eternal Tao. The name that can be spoken is not the eternal Name. End quote. So, what knowledge is available about the Tao? Well, the Taoist philosophers emphasize over and over again that the true Tao is an all-encompassing force that is beyond our comprehension and cannot be perceived by the senses. And even though we can never grasp the true Tao, the goal is to live in agreement with it, which is strikingly similar to the Stoic approach to nature. So, how do we live in harmony with the Way? Taoist literature doesn’t really give one practical method to achieve this. However, we can find many clues that point to achieving stillness of mind, curbing the senses, being humble, and the cessation of striving, in order to open ourselves up to the workings of the universe. This stillness of mind doesn’t necessarily mean that we sit down somewhere with our eyes closed. The Taoists observe that stillness of mind can be combined with action, and if we are completely in the present moment, our actions will go effortlessly, without friction and accompanied by a razor sharp focus. So much so, that it’s almost ecstatic. In his biography, retired professional basketball player Bill Russell writes: “It was almost as if we were playing in slow motion. During those spells I could almost sense how the next play would develop and where the next shot would be taken.” The Taoist work Zhuangzi contains a story about a cook named Ting who engages in his work while in a state of flow. This grasped the attention of Lord When-Hui, who was amazed about how elegantly the cook cut up oxen. When he commented him on his skill, Cook Ting laid down his knife and replied: “What I care about is the Way, which goes beyond skill. When I first began cutting up oxen, all I could see was the ox itself. After three years I no longer saw the whole ox. And now, now I go at it by spirit and don’t look with my eyes. Perception and understanding have come to a stop and spirit moves where it wants. I go along with the natural makeup, strike in the big hollows, guide the knife through the big openings, and following things as they are. So I never touch the smallest ligament or tendon, much less a main joint.” An essential part of this story is the condition of the knife that the cook uses. He stated that good cooks change their knives every year because they cut and mediocre cooks change their knives every month because they hack. Cook Ting however, was using the same knife for nineteen years, because he used it with skill and subtlety. This story connects to another essential teaching of Taoism which is the power of gentleness. By forcing and striving, we might get the job done, but at the same time we spend much more energy than necessary and possibly suffer from collateral damage. On the other hand: someone in a state of flow approaches a task intelligently, knowing when to act and when not to, and finds a balance between action and non-action. It’s a matter of not too hot, not too cold. It’s the golden path between anxiety and boredom. The idea behind non-action goes against the Western ideal of forcing and working harder and harder to get results. We are encouraged to be ambitious, to take control and to strive. Meanwhile many people suffer from depression, anxiety disorders and sleep disorders. Are we burning ourselves out? We look down on passivity, and often mistake it for laziness. But these are different things. When we look at nature, ‘doing nothing’ makes way more sense than we tend to think. Results do not equal the amount of energy we spend. Results are the consequence of a series of actions. The funny thing about this, is that many of these actions come naturally and a task doesn’t need more human intervention than necessary to steer it into the right direction. Isn’t it so that many problems solve themselves? Taoism compares life to a river. The river already has a course or several courses, and once we find ourselves in that river, we can swim against the current, we can hold on to a branch or we can let go and go along with the stream. Most of our lives, we swim against the current and we don’t even realize it. Our mind believes that it can and should control the environment, in order to survive, which is kind of egocentric because the vast majority of processes within as well as outside ourselves are not in our control. I mean, let’s face it: we don’t control our bodily processes like digestion, blood flow or the healing of wounds. We don’t control other people, we don’t control the future. We don’t even control who we fall in love with and what people we find attractive. Everything outside our own faculties just goes into some direction. Sometimes forced by intelligence, but mostly in a natural course. When we flow along with the current, we align ourselves with this natural course. This is the path of least resistance; it gives nature a chance to unfold, without us resisting it. So, the Taoist way is rather navigating through the river instead of trying to control it; something that will never work. Another aspect of the river that characterizes Taoism, is the water itself. The characteristics of water are softness and humility that basically symbolize Taoist virtue. Here’s a quote from the Tao Te Ching: The supreme good is like water, which benefits all of creation without trying to compete with it. It gathers in unpopular places. Thus it is like the Tao. Water may be soft, but it overcomes hardness which we can see in the erosion of rock. And water not only seeks the lower places; it also has no purpose, no goal, no specific desire. Yet, it nourishes everything that it passes. It’s an incredible life force, that literally does God’s work, but without any ambition. Water is the softest and most yielding substance. Yet nothing is better than water, for overcoming the hard and rigid, because nothing can compete with it. If you’ve ever experienced a state of flow, there’s one thing that disappears and only comes back when the thinking mind takes back control. This is the focus on results, rather than the task at hand. This reminds me of the Stoic concept of ‘amor fati’, which recommends one to embrace the outcome, whatever it may be, and instead of worrying about the future, focusing on what’s in the present. No matter if you’re completely immersed in sports, writing, a video game or dancing; when you’re in a state of flow, you forget the results, the pressure, the anxieties about the future, the failings of the past. It’s just you and the task at hand. You are completely in the present. And the only way to do this, is by letting go. Letting go means stop swimming against the current, stop holding on to some branches. - Stop Trying to Get It And You'll Have It | The Backwards Law: Kind: captions Language: en What if we’d try not to think of a pink elephant. This probably won’t work. Because as soon as the pink elephant appears in our minds, it’s impossible to get rid of it by consciously not thinking about it. And the more we try to get rid of it, the more it persists. The elephant simile is commonly used to show how difficult it is to get rid of intrusive thoughts by force. But we could also use this simile as a metaphor for how we approach dissatisfaction with life. The pink elephant, in this case, represents our general dissatisfaction, which may manifest as negative emotions like sadness, stress, anger, or boredom. Ironically, the more we try to be less dissatisfied, the more dissatisfied we become. So could it be that this inclination to be so invested in becoming free from dissatisfaction, trying to be happy, trying to be content, is exactly the reason we aren’t? Here we see the paradox of willpower, which is the basis of ‘the law of reversed effort’ also referred to as ‘the backwards law’ by philosopher Alan Watts. The backwards law proposes that the more we pursue something, the more we achieve the opposite of what we truly want and the more disappointed we feel. Or simply put: the harder we try, the less likely we’ll succeed. On the flip side: when we stop trying, we’ll have what we want. So, if we want to stop thinking about the pink elephant, in this case, giving up our struggle and letting our ‘desire to get rid of it’ dry out is the paradoxical solution Instead of trying to remove the elephant from our thoughts forcefully, we let it dissipate by itself by leaving it alone. Now, how exactly does this backwards law work in practice? Or more specifically: how exactly do we get what we want, by not trying to get what we want? This video explores the backwards law and its paradoxical nature, as well as the cause of our ongoing dissatisfaction in life, and how we can liberate ourselves from it. How can we get what we want without trying to get it? This seems like an impossible and absurd way to operate; especially in a world where we’re used to striving and putting effort into getting what we wish. Willpower is a viable solution to obtain things in the external world. For example, if we want to get rich (in the monetary sense), it most likely takes effort to obtain a certain amount of money that’ll classify us as ‘rich’. And if we wish to run a marathon, we’ll need to put in the necessary effort to build our stamina up to the point that we can run such a long distance. But the backwards law isn’t so much not about worldly achievements - if anything, it transcends them. It’s about getting what we really, truly want. It’s the shortcut to the holy grail; the thing we’re all after; the goodie. But what is it? Is it wealth? Is it love? Is it friendship? Is it a long and healthy life? Even though such things are pleasurable; they’re just cheap imitations of the real thing. They are the things that we believe will lead us to what we seek. But, as the backwards law makes clear, the more we seek, the less we find. The more we chase these outside circumstances, the further we’ll be removed from what we truly desire. So, what do we desire? Do we desire happiness? And if so, what is happiness? Is it something that we acquire through things like love and material possessions? According to Alan Watts, we don’t know what we truly want because we cannot define it. I quote: “Why don’t you really know what you want? Two reasons that you don’t really know what you want. Number one: you have it. Number two: you don’t know yourself, because you never can. The Godhead is never an object of its own knowledge, just as a knife doesn’t cut itself, fire doesn’t burn itself, light doesn’t illuminate itself.” End quote. So, could it be that what we seek is obscured by our search for it? And that we’re searching for something that we cannot define? But if that’s the case: why do we keep searching? The human predicament is a collective delusion which tells us that obtaining external things or changing external circumstances, from objects to money, to adjustments of the body to changes of scenery, will fundamentally release us from our sense of lack. The backwards law shows us that the opposite is the case. We feel lacking because of our discontent with current circumstances. The greater our discontent, the more we suffer. The greater change we need to be content, the less content we are. Imagine that you’ve set yourself a goal, which is that you want to become a millionaire, believing that this will make you happy. Setting such a goal not only means that it takes a lot of effort to reach contentment; it also means that being so far removed from that goal makes you unhappy because you realize how inadequate you are compared to what you want to be. Or how bestselling author Mark Manson put it: [..] pursuing something only reinforces the fact that you lack it in the first place. The more you desperately want to be rich, the more poor and unworthy you feel, regardless of how much money you actually make. So, if you’d increase the amount of money necessary to be happy, you’ll feel even more inadequate and subsequently more miserable. But if you’d significantly lower the threshold, your feeling of inadequacy will decrease, as the goalpost is moved much closer to where you are. Nevertheless, we still choose to set the bar high; oftentimes far above our current position, and by doing so our feeling of inadequacy is deep and persisting. The human tendency to continually pursue more as a cure for the itch, while simultaneously maintaining that itch by that very pursuit, seems illogical. And that’s precisely the case according to German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer. Schopenhauer concluded that we want what we want because, like anything else in the universe, we are representations of the will-to-live or, simply, the will. Schopenhauer argued that the ‘will’ is an illogical, directionless, continual striving that causes us to live a life of suffering that cannot be ended by anything that the world has to offer. Because of this, we pathologically want more than we need, driven by an incessant sense of lack. The mind perceives lack because it believes that the present moment is not enough; something is missing, but it doesn’t know what. And thus, we keep escaping what is, into situations that we perceive as more pleasurable. But when we get there, we eventually find ourselves in the same dissatisfied state that we tried to escape. Schopenhauer stated, and I quote: “Thus also every keen pleasure is an error and an illusion, for no attained wish can give lasting satisfaction.” According to Schopenhauer, the will is why we strive; the will is why we seek. But following it never satisfies, because the will itself is the very thing that keeps us from getting what we want. Schopenhauer argued that the only way to be truly content is the negation of the will, which leads to a blissful, empty state, free of striving. In other words: stop trying to get it and you’ll have it. He does not store, and therefore he has a superabundance; he looks solitary, but has a multitude around him. In his conducting of himself he is easy and leisurely and wastes nothing. He does nothing, and laughs at the clever and ingenious. Men all seek for happiness, but he feels complete in his imperfect condition. Accept imperfection and you feel perfect. Accept loneliness and you feel content alone. Try to be perfect and you’re imperfect. Try not to be lonely, and you’re miserable by yourself. Accepting a negative experience is a positive experience. But fighting a negative experience means that you suffer twice. “When you try to stay on the surface of the water, you sink; but when you try to sink, you float,” Alan Watts stated. In the same way, when you try to fall asleep, your effort will keep you awake. Only when you stop trying, you’ll doze off. And when you hold your breath, you’ll lose it. But when you let it go, it continues on its own. When we stop trying to be happy, we’ll be happy because there’s nothing we need beyond what is. When we stop trying to be rich, we’ll live in abundance because we’re content with what we have and anything on top of that is a bonus. Thus, the only way to have what we want is not to want it. And that’s what the backwards law teaches us. There’s a Zen-story that illustrates this paradoxical idea by explaining how we can clear cloudy water. Imagine there’s a pond with cloudy water and we want to see its floor. We can stir the water or try to remove the cloudiness with our hands, but this won’t work. The only way to see its floor is by doing nothing until the cloudiness subsides and the water is clear. The cloudiness represents our desires, our thoughts, our dissatisfaction. The stirring in the water and attempts to remove the cloudiness represent our grasping for happiness. ‘Seeing the floor’ represents contentment, which only happens when we leave the water alone and let the cloudiness subside by itself. Hence, stop trying to get it and you’ll have it. Being aware of the workings of the backwards law doesn’t mean that we should never set goals, never have ambitions, or never pursue change. There’s probably an endless amount of reasons why we should make a change, and shouldn’t accept the status quo. However, the backwards law does teach us not to be fooled by the idea that the pursuit of happiness leads to happiness. It’s quite the opposite. And with that knowledge, we’re able to enter that blissful state of ‘not wanting’ a bit more often. Because, as Alan Watts stated: “The mystery of life is not a problem to be solved but a reality to be experienced.” Thank you for watching.

The classic example here is productivity. Working for two hours is probably going to be twice as productive as working for one. Working for four might be twice as productive as two. That is the more effort you put into doing something, the more you will fail to do it. And how do we do this? You do this by relinquishing control, not because you feel powerless, but because you are powerful, because you have decided to let go of things that are beyond your control. You decide to accept that sometimes people will not like you but you engage with them anyway; that sometimes you will not feel confident, but you do the thing anyway; that sometimes you will not be happy, but you'll get out of bed anyway. You are consuming them. [music] You need them to behave in a certain way to make you feel safe. You become jealous, possessive, and controlling. You are saying you must fit into the script I have written for you. That is not love. That is hostage taking. Detachment allows you to look at the person and say, "I love you as you are. You are free [music] to stay and you are free to go. You are free to be yourself because my happiness does not depend on your compliance." That is a dangerous level of freedom. It makes you magnetic. [music] People run away from neediness, but they run toward freedom. When you no longer need people to validate you, you become a sanctuary for them. You become the one person in their life who isn't trying to take something from them. Let us apply this to the thing that keeps most of you awake at night. The spotlight effect. We are social animals. We evolved in tribes of 50 to 150 people. In the ancient world, if the tribe rejected you, you died. If you are exiled, you starved or were eaten by predators. [music] They are not judging your car. Why? Because they are too busy worrying about what you think of them. [music] We are all walking around trapped in our own private movies starring as the main character. Everyone else is just an extra in the background. [music] You can be a villain and someone will still love you. Character is what you do in the dark when nobody is watching. Reputation is just the gossip in the light.   8. @Sydardta [3 likes]: Alan Watts discusses Wu Wei, the concept of effortless action, in many of his talks and writings. In the context of a relationship where trust is gone but love is still there, Wu Wei can be applied in several ways:

• Accepting the situation: The first step is to accept that trust has been broken and that the relationship is in a difficult place. This doesn't mean giving up, but it does mean letting go of the need to control the situation or force things to be different.

• Practicing non-attachment: Wu Wei emphasizes non-attachment, which means not clinging to outcomes or trying to force things to happen in a certain way. In a relationship, this means being willing to let go of expectations and simply being present with the person you love, without trying to change them or control their behavior.

• Acting with compassion: Wu Wei also teaches us to act with compassion, which means understanding the other person's perspective and trying to see things from their point of view. In a relationship, this means being patient, forgiving, and willing to communicate openly and honestly.

• Letting go of the past: Wu Wei reminds us that the past is gone and cannot be changed. In a relationship, this means letting go of past hurts and resentments and focusing on the present moment.

Of course, applying Wu Wei in a relationship is not always easy. It requires a lot of patience, self-awareness, and willingness to forgive. But if both partners are committed to working things out, Wu Wei can be a powerful tool for healing and rebuilding trust.

Here are some specific examples of how Wu Wei can be applied in a relationship where trust is gone but love is still there:

• Instead of trying to force your partner to talk about what happened, simply be present and listen without judgment when they are ready to talk.

• Instead of trying to control your partner's behavior, focus on controlling your own reactions.

• Instead of dwelling on the past, focus on creating positive experiences together in the present.

• Instead of trying to change your partner, focus on accepting them for who they are.

Remember, Wu Wei is not about giving up or doing nothing. It is about acting with wisdom and compassion, and letting go of the things that are beyond our control.

If you are looking for more information on Wu Wei, I recommend reading the following books:

• Tao Te Ching by Lao Tzu

• The Way of Zen by Alan Watts

• Effortless Action by Jia-Shan

- Social Benefits of Alcohol | Edward Slingerland: Kind: captions Language: en - And so alcohol has a lot of different effects. The journalist Steven Brown has called it a pharmacological hand grenade. It just kinda goes in and starts hitting all the buttons at once. It's really, it's a messy drug. So it is in various timings and ways it simulates the effects of meth and cocaine. Prozac, Valium, opium, it's doing all of these things and at various points as your BAC increases. But crucially in what's gonna be crucial for the story I'm telling today is that it depresses the prefrontal cortex. It depresses the motor cortex as well which is why you shouldn't drive and you have trouble speaking at a certain point of inebriation. But crucially it's down regulating that part of our brain temporarily. And the nice thing is it does it gently, it does it predictably, and it does it with pretty short half life. You recover very quickly. So it's actually a brilliant technology for for taking the PFC offline temporarily. And what does that give you? It gives you creativity. So there's this association you see across the world throughout history of creative types, artists, writers, poets, with alcohol. You see it in ancient China, you see it in in the ancient mid east, you see it in the present day. This is not a myth. There actually is a very good reason why alcohol is associated with creativity in artists, it's because it actually does make us more creative by down regulating the prefrontal cortex. Now in terms of direct evidence of this there's not a whole lot right now. This is a nice study I like by Michael Andrews looking at correlation. He is taking advantage, he's an economist, and he took advantage of this great natural experiment, American prohibition. So we tend to think of prohibition as something that happened all at once at the federal level, just suddenly no one in America could drink. And it wasn't like that at all, it actually took a really long time to impose prohibition and it was imposed piecemeal at the county level. So he was able to look at county level data. And what he was looking at was patent applications as a proxy for innovation. And he could look at patent applications And what he saw is that when you impose prohibition on a county patent applications plunge, collective innovation plunges. And then it slowly recovers, it took about three years to get back to pre-prohibition levels. His hypothesis is speakeasys is why that happened. So basically (audience laughing) prohibition comes in, you can't drink socially anymore, innovation goes down and it goes down until people figure how to work around. And the work around was figuring out a new way to drink socially. So social drinking seems to be related to innovation, group innovation in this sense. There's also one nice direct study that shows that, so this is a actually not just correlational, it's causation, that if you take subjects and you give them a real alcoholic drink as opposed to a fake alcoholic drink they're more creative, and their creativity peaks at about 0.08. So that's about when you have a nice buzz on when you shouldn't operate a motor vehicle. But that seems to be the spot where you still have enough cognitive control to actually think coherently and do things that are useful, but you've been loosened up. The hold of the PFC has been loosened upon you in a certain way. So creativity is one of the really important functions of alcohol. Another strange thing about us compared to other primates is that we are communal. We're dependent on other people in a way that no other primate is. And to get anything useful done we need to trust one another. We need to engage in long-term cooperative tasks that require trust. And when we embark upon these tasks we run into various types of cooperation dilemmas. And these go under different types of names. You prisoners have dilemma, tragedy of the commons. They have the same structure though. You get the best payoff if you trust and you cooperate. The problem is, and this is a crucial part of the structure of these dilemmas, I don't know in advance whether or not you're gonna cooperate with me. And if you don't cooperate, if you defect as economists put it, I'm screwed. (Edward laughs) I get zero, you get a great payoff. And so for a rational self-interested agent in a prisoner's dilemma game the only strategy is to defect. So everyone defects and everybody gets that kinda bummer mutual defection outcome. In real life people solve this all the time. We're constantly solving prisoners' dilemmas in our real life. And we do it because we're not rational self interested agents, we're emotional. And we use emotions to help solve these dilemmas. We have emotions like honor, like loyalty, like trust that allow us, that bind us to each other in a certain way that prevent defections from happening. So emotions, the economist Robert Frank has a great book called "Passions Within Reason" where he explains that these love and honor and these things, they're approximately irrational. So in your actual psychology they're not rational but they have this kind of long-term rationality on an evolutionary scale. So we use these emotions, and because emotions help us cooperate we use them as cues to know who is a good cooperator and who's not. So when we're deciding whether or not to trust someone we look at their emotional expressions. This is a safety net we have in cooperation. I meet you and you genuinely are happy to meet me. How do I know you're genuinely happy? 'Cause you have that smile on the left and not the one on the right. The left one is a Duchenne smile, completely different muscle system not under typically under voluntary control. That's the smile you make when you're serving people in a restaurant or something, you have to be nice to them. We like the one on the left, we don't like the one on the right. So we use emotional displays as a way to know whether or not to trust people. This opens up this this possible risk though that people could be faking it. The soft spot here again is a prefrontal cortex. In order to lie, in order to cheat, in order to calculate you need your prefrontal cortex in top shape. Lying is very difficult cognitively right? You have to keep in track in your mind both what's true and what's what you're telling the person. You have to suppress emotions that have to do with the false thing that you're not telling them about. You need your PFC in top shape. What's also interesting is when the PFC is in top shape we're not as good at detecting lies. It's only when we're relaxed that we actually take in more information. So let's target the prefrontal cortex with what? With our good old friend alcohol. Right (Edward laughs) down regulates prefrontal cortex, it makes it harder for us to lie, it makes us easier for us to detect lies, and it's also simultaneously boosting some hormones like serotonin that make us less likely to cheat. So it's enhancing these kinda pro social hormones in human beings. So this is why when people, potentially hostile adults meet and have to come to some kind of agreement, they shake hands. And they're showing I'm not carrying a weapon. When you meet with someone and you do a couple of shots you're saying "I no longer have a prefrontal cortex. "I am cognitively disarming (audience laughs) "and putting my prefrontal cortex on the table. "You can trust me." This is why from ancient China to ancient Greece, alcohol is always at the center of banquets, of treaty negotiations, anything where you have people with potentially differing interests having to agree on something. All the way up to Nixon told his Chinese counterpart "if we drank enough Maotai we could do anything" right? This idea that if we just disarm cognitively we can solve these problems. And people use this informally all the time. So a cocktail party, a mixer, you're having to meet new people, you wanna cognitively disarm. So we're simultaneously decreasing our inhibitions and increasing these kind of pro social chemicals that help us like each other, like ourselves more, and like each other's more. So alcohol plays this really important tool in helping people bond, at helping people cooperate. This is also why when Skype was invented, remember back then? So this is one of the important functions of alcohol. So in "Drunk" I walk through these functional and important benefits of alcohol. But the important point is that you don't wanna lose sight of the cost of alcohol. It's a dangerous substance. It's estimated that up to 15% of the human population is prone to alcoholism. But the taste for alcohol has been preserved in our species because there are these countervailing benefits.

- The case for drinking: Kind: captions Language: en-US We have co-evolved with alcohol. - Trying Not to Try by Edward Slingerland: 6 Minute Summary: Kind: captions Language: en Edward Slingerland Trying Not to Try: Ancient China, Modern Science, and the Power of Spontaneity Introduction Discover the ancient Chinese concept of wu-wei and its astonishing effects on personal well-being and success. The book summary of 'Trying Not to Try: Ancient China, Modern Science, and the Power of Spontaneity' delves into various philosophical schools of thought, such as Taoism and Confucianism, and how they view achieving this state of 'effortless acting.' Explore the intricate balance between rational thought and instinct, and how melding these two aspects can lead to an intelligent spontaneity that makes work more enjoyable and efficient. Moreover, learn about the concept of 'de,' a unique form of power and charisma that arises from being in touch with your unconscious mind. Wu-Wei: The Art of Effortless Action Wu-wei, a Chinese philosophy that celebrates the art of effortless action, involves a harmonious relationship between the body and mind. When the two are brought together, they work as one, leading to intelligent spontaneity and fluidity in one's actions. Wu-wei makes you whole, guiding you purely by instinct, resulting in work that portrays beauty, sincerity, and ease of the process. The concept is not limited to the Chinese philosophy of Taoism, as one can experience it during any activity that makes them entirely absorbed and one with the process itself. The Power of Wu-Wei and De Wu-wei, the ancient Chinese concept of effortless action, when combined with de, or power and charisma, leads to a perfectly spontaneous mindset that allows individuals to act from their natural instincts. This concept is connected to The Way, a journey that leads to becoming a perfect human being. Wu-wei and de make leaders compelling without the need for threats and make average people attractive and likeable. People with de are in touch with their unconscious mind, which allows them to act from their natural instincts. Being in the flow, as defined by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, is similar to being in touch with de. However, in the Chinese conception, you are encouraged to move with ease throughout life, avoiding any difficulties that might harm your spirit. The benefits of wu-wei and de are far-reaching and can transport individuals to a perfectly spontaneous mindset that aligns with The Way. Confucianism's Path to Wu-Wei Confucius believed that reaching wu-wei required improving one's conscious mind through education and effort. This was achieved by practicing strict behavior and taking part in rituals, which assigned roles to participants with specific duties. By cultivating the power of the subconscious mind through conscious repetition, one can eventually achieve wu-wei. Confucianism's approach emphasizes the importance of improving one's willpower, behavior, and knowledge of past cultures. Confucian rituals taught people social manners and provided a clear repertoire for achieving wu-wei. Laozi's Philosophy of Going Home Laozi, the founder of Taoism, believed that the path to heaven is to forget societal teachings and return to human nature. He advocated for people to follow their basic desires by thinking less consciously and more unconsciously. In this state, people can experience a state similar to runner's high, where the brain downregulates conscious thinking and puts individuals on a blissful autopilot. Laozi believed in wu-wei, which means doing absolutely nothing. His goal was for individuals to connect with a raw version of themselves and return "home" to their true nature. Finding Wu-Wei Through Mencius and Zhuangzi Mencius and Zhuangzi offer alternative philosophies to Confucianism and Taoism, proposing a middle way to achieve wu-wei, the state of effortless action. Mencius believed that one already possessed the virtue needed for wu-wei, and a wise teacher could help one find and nurture it. Zhuangzi encouraged abandoning the dichotomy of right and wrong and adopting a neutral stance toward all things. The goal was to attain calmness, flexibility, and freedom from judgment to be ever-ready for change. Both philosophies emphasized the power of imagination in transforming behavior and achieving Wu-Wei: Living a Sincere Life Wu-Wei is a state of complete spontaneity and unselfconsciousness, but to achieve it, sincerity is crucial. The book explains that it's not enough to say you are generous; instead, you need to guide your whole life by the principle of generosity and dedicate yourself to it in everything you do. To attain the sincere flow of wu-wei, choose one of the action-oriented strategies espoused by Chinese thinkers, practice that mode until it becomes sincere, and pervades your entire character. The book suggests shaping yourself to uncover an underlying purpose that becomes the foundation for your practice. Uncover this purpose, and you'll be able to live a life that's wholeheartedly sincere. Practice physical activities, visualization, and meditation to achieve this state. Don't worry if you're not into complex theories, just give it a try, and you too can live the life you want and enjoy every moment of it. Final Recap Understanding and utilizing the concepts of wu-wei and de can benefit both personal and professional aspects of your life. By allowing your mind and body to work as one, you unlock numerous possibilities to achieve your goals effortlessly. Following in the footsteps of ancient Chinese philosophers, choose a strategy that aligns with your character and values. Through practice and perseverance, you can reach a state of sincerity and self-awareness that will help you create a more fulfilling and harmonious life. Embrace the power of spontaneity and the wisdom of the ancient Chinese to live a life that's true to yourself, with the added beauty of effortless flow.
