- Unraveling Zhuangzi: Kind: captions Language: en Welcome back everyone to The Explainer. I am absolutely thrilled you're here today because, well, we're going to do something a little bit different. We are going to solve a historical mystery, and in the process, we're going to unlock an incredibly modern anti-hustle philosophy from ancient China. Seriously, if you are feeling burnt out, over-scheduled, or just kind of trapped by the endless expectations of modern life, the ancient genius we're looking at today might just be the exact cure you need. Okay, let's dive right into this. If you were digging through older historical timelines, or, you know, dusty old encyclopedias, you might actually stumble upon this exact garbled phrase, "Chuang Tzu, founder of Chinese Monist religious philosophy." I mean, it sounds incredibly dry, super academic, and honestly, a bit intimidating. But the truth, this outdated label completely misrepresents one of the most brilliant, playful, and deeply skeptical minds in all of human history. Let's clear up that confusion right away. That weird Chuang Tzu spelling is actually just a distortion from an old, clunky English translation system for Chinese called Wade-Giles. The actual historical figure is Zhuang Zhou, who is most commonly known as Master Zhuang or Zhuang Zhou. And contrary to those old, dusty texts, he wasn't the absolute founder of Taoism. That title traditionally belongs to Laozi and the Daodejing. Nor was he a strict Monist just trying to push some rigid one-substance doctrine. Actually, scratch that. It's more like he was an incredibly influential interpreter of Taoist thought who absolutely loved to playfully dissolve our rigid divisions between right and wrong, dream and waking, useful and useless. Section 1, Warring States chaos, a violent age. To truly understand how radical his ideas were, we have to grasp the world he was living in. Zhuangzi lived roughly between 369 and 286 BCE. This was right in the thick of the Warring States period. Now, while his personal biographical record is pretty brief, and honestly, a bit legendary, we know for an absolute fact he lived in a violently chaotic age. China wasn't unified yet. You had massive competing states like Chin, Chu, and Chi constantly battling for supremacy, power, and territory. It was an era of high anxiety and constant survival pressure. And because the world felt like it was totally falling apart, everyone had a theory on how to fix it. This led to what's called the Hundred Schools of Thought. You had the Confucians arguing for strict ritual and family order. You had the Mohists pushing for practical benefits and anti-war policies. You had the Legalists demanding hardcore laws and state discipline. It was basically a loud, crowded room of competing ideologies. But Zhuangzi's unique Daoist approach completely different. Instead of screaming his doctrine the loudest, his response was to just step back and ask, "Why is everyone so utterly sure that their viewpoint is the final absolute truth?" Section two, the Dao and transformation, the flow of things. That skeptical step-back approach brings us to the core concept that anchors his entire worldview. Now, what's really interesting here is the irony. We are giving Dao a firm definition, translating it as the way or the spontaneous transforming process of nature, but Zhuangzi himself constantly warned us that the deepest Dao cannot actually be captured by ordinary human language. It's not some strict law handed down by a king. It's the living, breathing movement of the universe. And the truly wise person, they don't try to dominate it, they learn to move right along with it. And we learn how to move with it by reading his book, appropriately titled the Zhuangzi. It's made up of 33 chapters divided into inner, outer, and miscellaneous sections, with the first seven inner chapters being the ones most closely tied to him personally. But listen, if you open this book, do not expect a dry textbook. No way. It is a wild forest of stories, jokes, talking animals, and bizarre paradoxes. It is literally literary philosophy at its absolute finest. Section three, butterflies and useless trees, shifting perspectives. So, how exactly does a genius like this teach? Definitely not through step-by-step logical proofs. He uses unforgettable, mind-bending parables. This brings us to his most famous story, the butterfly dream. Zhuangzi falls asleep and dreams he is a butterfly, fluttering around entirely unaware of being a human. But, when he wakes up, he's struck by a profound question. Was he a man dreaming he was a butterfly, or is he right now a butterfly dreaming he is a man? He doesn't offer a rigid scientific theory to solve this. Instead, he uses wonder to challenge our fixed sense of identity, reminding us that reality from the inside is highly subjective. And this brilliant mindset completely shifted how he viewed societal pressures, too. Think about it. Society heavily values the straight, useful tree, right? But, what happens to it? Boom, it gets chopped down by carpenters. The twisted, gnarly on the other hand, is deemed completely useless by society. But, because it's useless, no one cuts it down, it survives, it grows huge, and it lives in total peace. He literally turns our standard categories upside down, showing us that being ignored by rulers and bosses can actually be the ultimate freedom. He pushes this idea of perspective even further in a famous debate with his friend Huizi. They're walking by a river, and Zhuangzi casually notes how happy the fish are. Huizi immediately challenges him, saying, "You aren't a fish. How can you possibly know the happiness of fish?" The playful argument that follows is a master class in relativism. Zhuangzi's reminding us that small birds, giant birds, humans, and fish all experience reality in vastly different ways. Assuming the human viewpoint is the only valid one, well, that's just sheer arrogance. Section four, Wu Wei and unforced action, applying the philosophy. So, shifting our perspective sounds great in theory, but how do we actually apply this? How do we navigate a demanding, stressful world without getting chopped down like that street tree? Zhuangzi gives us the ultimate practical example with the story of Cook Ding. Ding is a butcher carving an ox for a ruler. Now, a novice butcher just hacks aggressively, ruining his knife, constantly fighting the animal's structure. But, Cook Ding, he is a master. After years of deep practice, he doesn't hack it all. He lets his knife just glide effortlessly through the natural empty spaces in the joints. His action isn't strained or overthought. It's perfectly attuned to the exact situation in front of him. This illustrates an absolutely crucial concept, wu wei. It's so often poorly translated as non-action or doing nothing, but that's just wrong. As Cook Ding shows us, wu wei is definitely not laziness. It is acting without forced, artificial, ego-driven struggle. It's intelligent ease. It means relaxing our deeply human obsession with control, and instead moving smoothly with the grain of reality. And you can see how this philosophy bleeds directly into his political views. You've got the Confucians and Legalists completely obsessed with perfect rules, rituals, and political ambition. But, Zhuangzi, he championed spontaneity. He was famously suspicious of power. In fact, when a king sent messengers to offer him a highly prestigious official post, Zhuangzi essentially told them to go away, saying he'd rather be alive and dragging his tail in the mud than honored and trapped inside a royal court. He firmly believed that human rules trapped the living spirit. Section five, death, transformation, and legacy, and natural flow. Now, he didn't just apply this flowing philosophy to careers and politics. He applied it to the ultimate human fear, profoundly shaping how millions of people would come to understand life and legacy. His historical footprint is massive. He expanded Taoism with incredible humor and literary genius. His concepts gave Chinese Buddhism the exact language it needed to explain things like emptiness and non-attachment. Even his rivals, the Neo-Confucians, deeply engaged with his work centuries later. But perhaps the most striking thing is his view on death. When his own wife died, he initially mourned, but then he stopped, realizing that life and death are simply natural transformations of chi or energy. It's a challenging yet profoundly beautiful acceptance of the flow of all things. Seasons change, bodies change, the Tao continues. Section six, Zhuangzi's modern relevance, overcoming the hustle. Let's be real. This isn't just dusty ancient history. Let's bring this right back to today, to your life. Zhuangzi is quite literally the ultimate medicine for modern burnout. In a world completely obsessed with the hustle, with grades, status, relentless ambition, and these super rigid categories of what makes a person Zhuangzi is the ancient philosopher who sounds like he's just laughing at overconfident adults. He reminds us that our intellectual arrogance is a trap and that we aren't separate from nature. We are part of the exact same Tao as the rivers and the wind. Which leaves us with this final provocative thought to ponder today. Are you living freely? Or are you trapped by other people's labels? Are you exhausting yourself trying to be the straight tree that gets chopped down for society's use? Or can you find the courage to be just a little bit useless and wander freely within life's mystery? Think about that as you go about your week. Thank you so much for joining me on the Explainer and I will see you next time as we continue to map out the world's most fascinating ideas.

You see skyscrapers in the distance,&nbsp;&nbsp; a Hindu temple on your left, a coin laundry&nbsp; on your right, and a subway station in front&nbsp;&nbsp; of you. You see people walking around,&nbsp; trees and plants decorating the sidewalks,&nbsp;&nbsp; and cars driving on the insanely clean streets. There’s much to see in Singapore. It’s a colorful,&nbsp;&nbsp; diverse place. But as you walk through&nbsp; its streets, are you paying attention&nbsp;&nbsp; to what isn’t there? Are you aware of the&nbsp; spaces around and within everything you&nbsp;&nbsp; see? These questions may seem strange, but the&nbsp; Taoists argued that emptiness is as much a part&nbsp;&nbsp; of things as their physical form. In fact, it&nbsp; is often emptiness that makes them useful. Thirty spokes are joined together in a wheel, but it is the center hole that allows the wheel to function. We mold clay into a pot, but it is the emptiness inside that makes the vessel useful. ...according to the Tao Te Ching. When we think about it, without emptiness none&nbsp;&nbsp; of the things we observe in our world can really&nbsp; exist, as the ancient Greek philosopher Parmenides&nbsp;&nbsp; already suggested. We need empty space. We need&nbsp; it for movement, for separation between objects&nbsp;&nbsp; and beings, for making anything functional. Take a house, for example. We may put great&nbsp;&nbsp; emphasis on the materials used to build it,&nbsp; such as its concrete walls, wooden doors,&nbsp;&nbsp; or soundproof windows. We want the foundation&nbsp; to be strong, the roof to be durable. But,&nbsp;&nbsp; as Lao Tzu suggested, isn’t the emptiness inside&nbsp; that makes it livable? Sure, we use the materials&nbsp;&nbsp; to put the house together, but it’s mainly&nbsp; the empty spaces between them that we use. The same goes for anything in a city, like&nbsp; Singapore: it’s the empty space within&nbsp;&nbsp; subway stations that allows us to enter,&nbsp; walk to the platforms, and board trains.&nbsp;&nbsp; It allows these trains to move within&nbsp; the tunnels in the first place. So, emptiness turns out to be highly&nbsp; essential for our existence. Okay. That’s a nice observation. But how could&nbsp; this notion help us in our daily affairs? The&nbsp;&nbsp; ancient Taoist texts show that the significance of&nbsp; emptiness isn’t limited to the mere functionality&nbsp;&nbsp; of objects in the world; it also applies to&nbsp; the workings of our minds and how we feel. From a Taoist perspective, the problem with&nbsp; many people is that their minds are simply&nbsp;&nbsp; ‘too full’. Let’s take a look. Give up intellectual learning and you will have no worries. Agreement and disagreement, are they really so different? Good and evil, are they really so far apart? What others fear, must I also fear? This nonsense is unending! In this translation by author&nbsp;&nbsp; and qigong teacher Solala Towler, is Lao Tzu&nbsp; advocating for full-blown anti-intellectualism? Not really, at least not the kind of&nbsp; anti-intellectualism we often see today,&nbsp;&nbsp; where people reject institutional systems of&nbsp; knowledge, sometimes for understandable reasons,&nbsp;&nbsp; only to replace them with influencer&nbsp; slogans, simplistic worldviews,&nbsp;&nbsp; and conspiracy narratives that lack evidence and&nbsp; reinforce personal biases. That, too, is a form of&nbsp;&nbsp; “intellectual learning,” but a pretty poor one. Lao Tzu does seem wary of intellectual pursuits,&nbsp;&nbsp; though. Gaining knowledge and immersing ourselves&nbsp; in countless categories, ideas, and theories is&nbsp;&nbsp; all fun and games, but these also occupy our&nbsp; minds. They can lead to worry and overthinking.&nbsp;&nbsp; We become attached to distinctions and conceptual&nbsp; frameworks, while reality itself may be far more&nbsp;&nbsp; fluid than our concepts suggest. Over time, we may begin to mistake our&nbsp;&nbsp; interpretations for reality itself. We develop&nbsp; strong opinions about what is good and evil,&nbsp;&nbsp; right and wrong, whom we should fear and whom we&nbsp; should welcome. Inevitably, these belief systems&nbsp;&nbsp; clash with those of others, something we can&nbsp; observe in many parts of the West today. When our minds are full and closed off, there&nbsp; is little room for new insights or different&nbsp;&nbsp; perspectives. But what if, even just temporarily,&nbsp; we’d empty our minds of existing beliefs? What&nbsp;&nbsp; if we’d just let go of what we know? What if we&nbsp; create space to see reality without immediately&nbsp;&nbsp; filtering it through the lens of what we&nbsp; already believe or assume to be true? From a Taoist perspective, this space creates&nbsp; a sense of openness, or xū (虚), a receptive&nbsp;&nbsp; state of mind that allows us to perceive&nbsp; reality more clearly, without being overly&nbsp;&nbsp; constrained by prior interpretations. “The empty apartment is filled with&nbsp;&nbsp; light through it.” ..said Zhuangzi. Like an empty room illuminated by&nbsp; light, an empty mind becomes more&nbsp;&nbsp; receptive to reality and direct experience. There’s another aspect to ‘emptiness of mind’;&nbsp;&nbsp; not so much the absence of knowledge, but the&nbsp; absence of all kinds of discursive activity.&nbsp;&nbsp; We tend to fill our minds with problems,&nbsp; seeking solutions, planning, plotting,&nbsp;&nbsp; sometimes in a very repetitive manner. Our minds&nbsp; become crowded and tense. And the more we try to&nbsp;&nbsp; force a good idea, the less we seem to succeed. Many of our best ideas emerge when we stop trying&nbsp;&nbsp; so hard. They arrive during a morning walk&nbsp; or in the shower. They come up when our&nbsp;&nbsp; minds are spacious; when there’s room for&nbsp; ideas to appear naturally. It is often the&nbsp;&nbsp; ‘emptiness of the mind’ in such moments that&nbsp; allows ideas to arise, rather than discursive&nbsp;&nbsp; thought trying to force them into existence. But there’s another dimension of mental emptiness&nbsp;&nbsp; that could benefit us, according to the ancient&nbsp; Taoist texts, which we’ll explore right now.&nbsp; Someone asked the Taoist philosopher Lieh-tzu why&nbsp; he valued ‘emptiness’. He answered as follows: “Most people like to be praised. They feel good&nbsp; when their accomplishments are acknowledged.&nbsp;&nbsp; However, I feel we would be better off if we&nbsp; were empty of attachments and not imprisoned&nbsp;&nbsp; by recognition, approval, and disapproval. In the&nbsp; long run, we’d have fewer things to worry about.&nbsp;&nbsp; That’s why I value emptiness.” End quote. Lieh-tzu saw what many spiritual traditions&nbsp; and philosophers have observed as well: a mind&nbsp;&nbsp; preoccupied with worldly concerns, described in&nbsp; the original text as “fame and profit,” or míng&nbsp;&nbsp; lì (名利), is not a very pleasant mind. It’s a mind&nbsp; full of worry; a mind that generates suffering. And let’s face it: pursuing fame often means&nbsp; constantly trying to please an audience. We&nbsp;&nbsp; end up doing and saying things with&nbsp; other people’s approval in mind. Obtaining praise usually takes a lot of effort.&nbsp; And most people want to keep the praise coming;&nbsp;&nbsp; they fear falling out of favor, so they&nbsp; keep watering it, hoping people will&nbsp;&nbsp; continue to adore them. And so, they have&nbsp; built themselves a prison; one based on&nbsp;&nbsp; “recognition, approval, and disapproval”. What’s even worse is that people’s opinions&nbsp;&nbsp; aren’t in their control, and they might fall out&nbsp; of favor anyway despite their efforts. So, there’s&nbsp;&nbsp; always the fear that they’ll lose the recognition&nbsp; and approval they spent so much time building,&nbsp;&nbsp; which, as we know, could happen in a heartbeat. A mind occupied with profit is another path to&nbsp;&nbsp; ongoing worry and anxiety. When we view life&nbsp; primarily through the lens of gain and loss,&nbsp;&nbsp; our well-being becomes tied to circumstances&nbsp; beyond our control. Success leads to satisfaction,&nbsp;&nbsp; while failure brings disappointment. And&nbsp; so we spend our days pursuing profit and&nbsp;&nbsp; guarding against loss, as our happiness depends&nbsp; on it. Often, that’s a stressful way to live. So, Lieh-tzu felt people would be better off&nbsp; if their minds were empty of such attachments.&nbsp;&nbsp; Pursuits of fame and wealth are worthless anyway,&nbsp; he claimed. And our so-called accomplishments&nbsp;&nbsp; rely so heavily on external circumstances that we&nbsp; might ask ourselves whether taking credit for them&nbsp;&nbsp; and parading them around is even fair. Better just let them go and quiet down,&nbsp;&nbsp; says Lieh-tzu. And by doing so, we might&nbsp; even reach the ultimate form of Taoist&nbsp;&nbsp; emptiness, which we’ll explore next. If you can empty your mind of all thoughts your heart will embrace the tranquility of peace. Watch the workings of all of creation, but contemplate their return to the source. When we’ve contemplated the value of emptiness,&nbsp;&nbsp; calmed our minds, and let go of desires for&nbsp; fame and profit, we could engage in the process&nbsp;&nbsp; Zhuangzi called the ‘fasting of the heart’. In ancient Chinese thought, the heart, xin (心),&nbsp;&nbsp; was seen as the center of both thinking&nbsp; and feeling, which is why Zhuangzi’s term&nbsp;&nbsp; is often translated as either “fasting&nbsp; of the heart” or “fasting of the mind.”&nbsp;&nbsp; In Chinese, it is called xinzhai (心齋). When our modern lives usually revolve around&nbsp;&nbsp; ‘gaining,’ such as gaining knowledge, gaining&nbsp; experiences, gaining money, or gaining power,&nbsp;&nbsp; the idea of the fasting of the heart is more&nbsp; about losing or forgetting. Instead of trying to&nbsp;&nbsp; get more, we take the weight off our shoulders,&nbsp; until there’s nothing left but… emptiness. In the Zhuangzi, Confucius&nbsp; describes the process as follows: “Don’t listen with your ears, listen with&nbsp; your mind. No, don’t listen with your mind,&nbsp;&nbsp; but listen with your spirit. Listening stops&nbsp; with the ears, the mind stops with recognition,&nbsp;&nbsp; but spirit is empty and waits on all things. The&nbsp; Way gathers in emptiness alone. Emptiness is the&nbsp;&nbsp; fasting of the mind.” The fasting of the heart is more than letting go&nbsp; of desires for success or reputation. It means&nbsp;&nbsp; letting go of outcomes, beliefs, ambitions, and&nbsp; even our sense of self. Rather than constantly&nbsp;&nbsp; judging things as good or bad, right or wrong, we&nbsp; remain open to a world that is always changing. This kind of mental clarity, so to speak,&nbsp; allows for spontaneous action. We can observe&nbsp;&nbsp; what is happening without distortion from&nbsp; preconceptions, expectations, or desires,&nbsp;&nbsp; and respond to what arises. It is an openness, an&nbsp; emptiness, that allows us to experience reality&nbsp;&nbsp; more directly. And this may even enhance&nbsp; our performance in certain situations. We can find an example of this in the Zhuangzi,&nbsp; which tells about a skilled archer who could&nbsp;&nbsp; easily hit the target when nothing was at&nbsp; stake. But when he competed for a prize,&nbsp;&nbsp; his thoughts about winning interfered with&nbsp; his ability to shoot. His mind was filled&nbsp;&nbsp; with desire, anxiety, and thoughts about&nbsp; the future, whereas before it was clear,&nbsp;&nbsp; allowing him to shoot with ease. From a Taoist perspective, the fasting&nbsp;&nbsp; of the mind brings us closer to the Tao,&nbsp; which lies at the very heart of Taoism.&nbsp;&nbsp; The Tao cannot be fully understood through&nbsp; concepts or intellectual analysis, yet it&nbsp;&nbsp; is ever-present and underlies all things. As we let go of our attachment to ideas, concepts,&nbsp;&nbsp; and discursive thought, we become more attuned&nbsp; to the greater process of which we are a part.&nbsp;&nbsp; Or as Sinologist Woei-Lien Chong wrote&nbsp; in her book about Taoist philosophy:&nbsp;&nbsp; “one with the breathing of the cosmos.” If you’re interested in Taoist philosophy,&nbsp;&nbsp; I’ve compiled a book of my ramblings&nbsp; inspired by ancient Taoist texts,&nbsp;&nbsp; titled Taoism for Inner Peace. Thank you for watching.

- The Less You Care, The Happier You’ll Be | Taoist Wisdom For An Overly Serious World: Kind: captions Language: en A long time ago, Confucius and his students&nbsp; walked on a road to the kingdom of Wei. They&nbsp;&nbsp; stumbled upon a hermit at least a hundred years&nbsp; old. The man was gathering some grain that farmers&nbsp;&nbsp; had dropped and he was singing while doing so.&nbsp; One of the students, a young man named Tzu-Kung,&nbsp;&nbsp; was confused. He couldn’t comprehend why the&nbsp; old hermit was so happy, as he must have been&nbsp;&nbsp; very poor and alone, having to scour for harvest&nbsp; scraps. Tzu-Kung walked over to the hermit and&nbsp;&nbsp; showed compassion for his sad fate. But the old&nbsp; man smiled and said: “Why do you feel sorry for&nbsp;&nbsp; me? Am I that pathetic in your eyes?” “Well,&nbsp; sir,” Tzu-Kung said, “I assumed you didn’t&nbsp;&nbsp; work hard in your younger years and didn’t care&nbsp; about success and status. And so you couldn’t&nbsp;&nbsp; find a wife and have children to look after you.&nbsp; You’re all alone. How could you laugh and sing?”&nbsp; “Listen, young man,” the hermit said, “I laugh&nbsp; and sing because I feel happy! If I had worked&nbsp;&nbsp; hard in my younger years, competing with others,&nbsp; I wouldn’t have gotten so old and healthy. And&nbsp;&nbsp; not having a wife and children? That’s great.&nbsp; I don’t have to worry about their lives either.&nbsp;&nbsp; It’s peaceful. Why shouldn’t I laugh and sing?” This story is from a Taoist scripture called&nbsp;&nbsp; Lieh Tzu. It shows a typical Taoist way of&nbsp; thinking, namely, that there’s always gain&nbsp;&nbsp; in what we perceive as loss. Even though the&nbsp; elderly man is not conventionally well-off,&nbsp;&nbsp; he is quite the archetypical “loser” in&nbsp; today’s language; he’s well aware of his&nbsp;&nbsp; many blessings in disguise. But for most people,&nbsp; it’s probably challenging to have this attitude.&nbsp;&nbsp; We’re easily swayed by societal standards&nbsp; and concerned with other people’s opinions.&nbsp; This is where Taoist philosophy becomes especially&nbsp; valuable. It contains the wisdom to worry less,&nbsp;&nbsp; not just about what other people&nbsp; think but about almost anything.&nbsp;&nbsp; Isn’t that something we need today? Just&nbsp; look around—distractions are everywhere,&nbsp;&nbsp; and times are changing rapidly. Life is stressful&nbsp; and demanding, with many suffering from burnout&nbsp;&nbsp; and depression and others on the verge. This video shares three insights from&nbsp;&nbsp; ancient Taoist sages to help you&nbsp; care less in an overly serious world. If you want to support Einzelgänger, consider&nbsp; joining my Patreon page, which allows access&nbsp;&nbsp; to ad-free videos and free merch. Thank&nbsp; you, and I hope you’ll enjoy this video. The Taoist sage Zhuangzi observed long ago&nbsp; how people are hung up on things like fame,&nbsp;&nbsp; wealth, and status. In his time, people pursued&nbsp; luxuries, such as expensive food and fine clothes,&nbsp;&nbsp; and traveled to far places to enjoy the sights.&nbsp; Today, we see nothing has changed. Moreover,&nbsp;&nbsp; our modern-day media constantly pressures&nbsp; us to live a high life. Our tendency to&nbsp;&nbsp; seek out that new, shiny thing, whether&nbsp; luxury or experience, is being exploited.&nbsp; The more lavish, the better. Society&nbsp; teaches us to have great careers,&nbsp;&nbsp; big houses, nice cars. We get raised under the&nbsp; imperative to be successful and, if possible,&nbsp;&nbsp; wealthy. Material success, status, and&nbsp; achievement are the metrics by which&nbsp;&nbsp; we decide people’s worth. It’s what&nbsp; the world “honors,” argues Zhuangzi. “If they do not got these things,&nbsp;&nbsp; they are very sorrowful and go on&nbsp; to be troubled with fears,” he said. Once you commit yourself to pursuing all these&nbsp; celebrated external things, it seems to be never&nbsp;&nbsp; enough. Once you get a nice car, you will likely&nbsp; want a better one. Once you have your dream house,&nbsp;&nbsp; things get old quickly; the luxury no longer feels&nbsp; that special. The euphoric happiness generated by&nbsp;&nbsp; this once so-much-desired (but pricey) house&nbsp; fades into normalcy. But despite not feeling&nbsp;&nbsp; much happier in the long run, you still have&nbsp; to make your mortgage payments. Over time,&nbsp;&nbsp; you become trapped—a slave to your possessions. From Zhuangzi’s viewpoint, this is a stressful&nbsp;&nbsp; mode of living. People living like this wear&nbsp; themselves out. “This is a stupid way to treat&nbsp;&nbsp; the body,” he stated. And isn’t he correct,&nbsp; looking at the rates of burnout, anxiety,&nbsp;&nbsp; and depression in modern-day societies? In pursuit&nbsp; of riches, we are wearing ourselves out. In the&nbsp;&nbsp; quest for fame on social media, we’re exploiting&nbsp; ourselves. We’re doing it because we think it&nbsp;&nbsp; makes us happy. Many do it so other people hold&nbsp; them in high esteem. Others do it to belong,&nbsp;&nbsp; but they’re nothing more than cogs in the&nbsp; consumerist machine: a never-ending pursuit&nbsp;&nbsp; of stuff and fame that never satisfies,&nbsp; rarely leading to lasting happiness;&nbsp;&nbsp; something ancient Greek philosopher Epicurus&nbsp; also realized, as he saw many of the things we&nbsp;&nbsp; pursue nowadays as unnecessary and vain. At the same time, Zhuangzi observed that&nbsp;&nbsp; people look down on poverty, bad reputation, and&nbsp; what we’d call “irrelevance” today. Nobody wants&nbsp;&nbsp; to be a nobody. You don’t want to be a loser,&nbsp; do you? Losers are the modern-day untouchables.&nbsp;&nbsp; These people don’t have the finest clothes,&nbsp; don’t eat oysters and caviar, and don’t get&nbsp;&nbsp; to see the many fabulous sights of the world.&nbsp; They are to be met with contempt and avoidance.&nbsp; But Zhuangzi said we can’t judge right&nbsp; and wrong by the world’s standards. He&nbsp; proposes “doing nothing,” as doing&nbsp; nothing leads to perfect enjoyment. “Heaven does nothing, and&nbsp; thence comes its serenity;&nbsp;&nbsp; Earth does nothing, and thence&nbsp; comes its rest,” he stated. We could ask ourselves: do all these external&nbsp; things truly make us happy? Or can happiness be&nbsp;&nbsp; found in the simplest things? Isn’t the mere&nbsp; cessation of trying to pursue happiness when&nbsp;&nbsp; happiness arises? The reason we’re unhappy seems&nbsp; to be that we try too hard to be happy. And we&nbsp;&nbsp; do so following a dead-end path. How about&nbsp; we stop striving and let enjoyment unfold? Our achievement society scares us into&nbsp; being useful, self-exploiting members&nbsp;&nbsp; of the capitalist system. We’re expected to be&nbsp; good for “something” to participate in the rat&nbsp;&nbsp; race and to be successful in what we do so we can&nbsp; respect ourselves and gain the respect of others.&nbsp; From the Taoist point of view, we’re all playing&nbsp; a silly game. We adopt specific beliefs, mark&nbsp;&nbsp; them as the truth, and act accordingly, taking&nbsp; it all very seriously. Hence, we care greatly&nbsp;&nbsp; about walking in line and what people think about&nbsp; us. People generally fear being disliked and seen&nbsp;&nbsp; as odd, worthless, or inadequate, whatever&nbsp; that means. Most people spend their lives&nbsp;&nbsp; conforming to what society values: having many&nbsp; friends, having a good job, starting a family,&nbsp;&nbsp; and being a useful member of society: “I’m&nbsp; a hard-working, god-fearing, freedom-loving&nbsp;&nbsp; American. And I’m proud of it!” Of course,&nbsp; if you earned your rank in the game, there’s&nbsp;&nbsp; no shame in looking down on those we didn’t. But as Zhuangzi said, we can’t judge right and&nbsp;&nbsp; wrong by the world’s standards. The majority may&nbsp; agree on something, but that doesn’t mean it’s a&nbsp;&nbsp; universal truth. Taoist sages generally love&nbsp; crushing conventional beliefs. For example,&nbsp;&nbsp; suppose everyone thinks that being ‘unambitious’&nbsp; is bad. As Zhuangzi might argue, because of this,&nbsp;&nbsp; people fret greatly about not being seen&nbsp; as unambitious. So, they chase promotions,&nbsp;&nbsp; flaunt their career ambitions, and spend&nbsp; hours discussing their new roles and future&nbsp;&nbsp; plans—just to prove to others that they’re&nbsp; driven and worthy of admiration. People who&nbsp;&nbsp; lack such aspirations are generally frowned&nbsp; upon. And for many, that’s frightening.&nbsp; But the Taoist sages challenge us to look&nbsp; beyond societal conditioning. In this case,&nbsp;&nbsp; we could ask ourselves: Is being unambitious&nbsp; truly bad? Is following your ambition really&nbsp;&nbsp; worth the daily stress? What if we choose&nbsp; not to be ambitious—or even refuse to be cogs&nbsp;&nbsp; in the machine? How about we become like the&nbsp; elderly hermit, turning our backs on societal&nbsp;&nbsp; expectations? Would we be worse off or not? What comes to mind is the story of the useless&nbsp;&nbsp; tree, one of the most profound parables that&nbsp; turns the world upside down in a Taoist fashion.&nbsp; Carpenter Shih and his apprentice&nbsp; once passed a massive oak standing by&nbsp;&nbsp; the village shrine. The oak’s branches could&nbsp; easily shelter hundreds of oxen during rainfall.&nbsp;&nbsp; Around the oak gathered dozens of people, amazed&nbsp; by its size and beauty. The apprentice said:&nbsp; “Wow, I’ve never seen such a beautiful tree. But&nbsp; you don’t even care to look at it. Why is that?”&nbsp;&nbsp; “Are you kidding me?” said the carpenter.&nbsp; “This tree is worthless! Can’t you see how&nbsp;&nbsp; crooked it is? Make boats of it, and they’ll&nbsp; sink; make closets or doors, and they’ll rot&nbsp;&nbsp; instantly! It’s useless!” That night, the carpenter&nbsp;&nbsp; dreamed the crooked tree spoke to him. “Listen, buddy,” the tree said. “I heard you talk.&nbsp;&nbsp; You think I’m worthless, not good for anything.&nbsp; And that’s true to an extent. Just look at the&nbsp;&nbsp; apple and orange trees. They’re useful. They bring&nbsp; about fruits, which is why people love them. But&nbsp;&nbsp; look at their existence. They’re being exploited.&nbsp; When their fruits are ripe, they’re subjected to&nbsp;&nbsp; abuse. Their big branches are broken off; they’re&nbsp; pulled and jerked around. And when they don’t&nbsp;&nbsp; produce anymore, they’re cut down. Do you see&nbsp; how their utility makes their lives miserable?&nbsp;&nbsp; They can’t even live out the full years Heaven&nbsp; intended for them. I, on the other hand, am of no&nbsp;&nbsp; use. And being useless turned out to be of great&nbsp; use to me. If I had been useful, would I’ve grown&nbsp;&nbsp; this big? I owe my long life to being useless.” As we see in the story, uselessness, which is&nbsp;&nbsp; generally seen as a bad trait (especially&nbsp; in our achievement society), was a benefit&nbsp;&nbsp; for the tree. It reminds us of the old hermit&nbsp; whose unfortunate life, by societal standards,&nbsp;&nbsp; hid a blessing in disguise. There’s always&nbsp; some gain in loss. The trick is to discover it. Pei-kung-tzu and Hsi-men-tzu, long-separated&nbsp; friends, met again one day. Pei-kung-tzu was&nbsp;&nbsp; astonished at how different their lives&nbsp; turned out. His old friend became wealthy,&nbsp;&nbsp; successful, and respected,&nbsp; but he turned out very poor,&nbsp;&nbsp; and most people didn’t like or trust him. Pei-kung-tzu complained, and I quote: “When we both took office in&nbsp; government, you were promoted,&nbsp;&nbsp; and I was dismissed. When we both farmed,&nbsp; even the earth cooperated with you and not&nbsp;&nbsp; with me. When we traded together, you made&nbsp; profits and I lost. This is really unfair!” End quote. He continued complaining about&nbsp;&nbsp; wearing old clothing, eating food usually&nbsp; given to pigs, living in a broken shack,&nbsp;&nbsp; and being unable to afford a cart. In contrast,&nbsp; his old friend ate the best foods, lived in a&nbsp;&nbsp; giant mansion, and traveled in a luxury vehicle.&nbsp; Didn’t they both have the same background and&nbsp;&nbsp; education? Why did their fates deviate so much? When Pei-kung-tzu confronted his old friend with&nbsp;&nbsp; this perceived unfairness, Hsi-men-tzu exploded,&nbsp; telling him that his success in life stems from&nbsp;&nbsp; being more virtuous and, therefore, more worthy&nbsp; in the eyes of others. Of course, Pei-kung-tzu&nbsp;&nbsp; felt depressed after this slap in the face and&nbsp; sought consolation from the village sage. The sage&nbsp;&nbsp; asked why Hsi-men-tzu insulted his old friend, who&nbsp; explained that Pei-kung-tzu simply couldn’t stand&nbsp;&nbsp; that he was less worthy than himself. But the sage&nbsp; corrected him, explaining that worthiness cannot&nbsp;&nbsp; be measured by social or political success.&nbsp; He had simply more luck in life. I quote: “You are successful in society not because you are&nbsp; particularly wise or virtuous but because you have&nbsp;&nbsp; luck in everything you do. On the other hand,&nbsp; Pei-kung-tzu’s failure to be recognized is not&nbsp;&nbsp; due to stupidity or lack of virtue. It’s because&nbsp; he does not have luck in everything he does.” When Pei-kung-tzu&nbsp;&nbsp; heard what the sage said to his old friend,&nbsp; he felt OK with his situation. He no longer&nbsp;&nbsp; let his lack of luck be a reason for unhappiness. The story shows us that embracing fate and finding&nbsp;&nbsp; contentment, whether rich or poor, successful or&nbsp; not, leads to inner peace. We often can’t do much&nbsp;&nbsp; about how things work out around us, but&nbsp; we can cultivate our attitudes toward these&nbsp;&nbsp; things. Usually, our best bet is to let things go&nbsp; their natural course and focus on how we navigate&nbsp;&nbsp; through them instead of trying to control them. Is there a more relaxing attitude in a fast-paced,&nbsp;&nbsp; stressful world than letting all these attachments&nbsp; and must-haves slide and take life however it&nbsp;&nbsp; comes? Who’s more successful? The wealthy&nbsp; person waking up dissatisfied every morning,&nbsp;&nbsp; always chasing more? Or the poor, waking up&nbsp; content, happy with whatever the Heavens give him? Thank you for watching.

- Reasons Not to Worry What Others Think: Kind: captions Language: en You have no responsibility to live up to what other people think you ought to accomplish. I have no responsibility to be like they expect me to be. It’s their mistake, not my failing. It’s generally a good idea to care about other people’s opinions to some degree, as they could contain some worthwhile insight. But focusing on them too much to the point that we spend hours and hours dwelling on what people might think can leave us in agony. It’s not only potentially harmful but also unnecessary. This video explains why based on several concepts from psychology and philosophy. (1) You’re giving away your power. The moment we let our joy depend on the validation by other people, we give away the power over our emotional states. With this attitude, it feels exhilarating when people fancy us. But when they don’t, we become sad and angry. Especially now, in the age of social media, many have made other people’s approval their focal point in life. Positive attention, then, becomes a requirement for happiness, which entirely depends on the whims of those we try to impress. It can even become an addiction. Many of the people that we try to impress we don’t even know. Moreover, many of them have ever-changing opinions, often without substance, or are downright ignorant. So why would we waste our time trying to make them like us? Chances are, we don’t even like them? Stoic philosopher Seneca said about this, and I quote: How mad is he who leaves the lecture-room in a happy frame of mind simply because of applause from the ignorant! Why do you take pleasure in being praised by men whom you yourself cannot praise? (2) It’s beyond your control. The problem with worry is that our minds try to control the uncontrollable. People’s opinions are ultimately not up to us, so there isn’t much we can do to stop them from disliking us. Now, this doesn’t mean that we cannot influence what other people think. As a variation to the dichotomy of control (a concept from Stoicism), professor of philosophy and author William B. Irvine proposed the trichotomy of control. The dichotomy of control as presented by Epictetus makes a distinction between the things that are within our control and things that aren’t. The trichotomy of control, however, offers three categories: Things over which we have complete control. Things over which we have no control at all. And things over which we have some but not complete control. Opinions of other people fall into the second and third categories. In some cases, there’s nothing we can do about what others think. For example, we cannot change what someone said to us in the past, and we cannot change our parents’ disapproval of us when they’re dead. But we can influence people in the present by our words and actions. But even though our behavior could be incredibly influential, the results are still not up to us. Therefore, worrying about what’s happening in the brains of others is futile, and we’re better off focusing on our own actions. (3) It’s a reflection of them - not you. Often, how people react to us directly reflects themselves and how they feel. When we incur hostility, indifference, or sadness, as a response to our actions or even to our very presence, it may not always be personal. Moreover, these people could be expressing parts of their unconscious without realizing it. Swiss psychiatrist Carl Jung called this phenomenon ‘projection’. Jung believed that people tend to repress unwanted aspects of themselves into the unconscious parts of the mind, which form, what he called, the Shadow. A consequence is that we unconsciously recognize in others what we recognize in ourselves. As we dislike in others what we dislike in ourselves, an adverse emotional reaction follows. Psychology Today describes projection as follows, Unconscious discomfort can lead people to attribute unacceptable feelings or impulses to someone else to avoid confronting them. Projection allows the difficult trait to be addressed without the individual fully recognizing it in themselves. End quote. Jung stated that projections change the world into a replica of one’s unknown face. We all see the world through a unique lens, and the unconscious plays a significant role in how we relate to our environment. Knowing this, we can put the opinions of other people into perspective. (4) You’re not the center of the universe. When we try to imagine the vastness of the universe, we begin to understand the insignificance of ourselves. We may experience ourselves as the center of it all because we see it exclusively through our eyes, but most would agree that we are not. But, of course, we never know. Solipsism is the idea that only one’s mind is sure to exist, as we cannot prove that the external world (including the minds of others) is real. To this day, one cannot experience the existence of other minds than one’s own. If your mind is indeed the only mind in existence, other people’s opinions are nothing but illusions. Thus, nothing to make a fuss about, as they aren’t real. But even though solipsism could be the reality, there seems to be a consensus that other minds do exist. If the latter is the case, then other people’s opinions are indeed real. But if all people have minds comparable to our own and are as immersed in their troubles as we are, then they’re probably not thinking about us as much as we’d believe. Moreover, most people are so busy concerning themselves with what others think of them that they don’t have time to take a good look at the very people they try to impress. In the grand scheme of things, opinions are incredibly brief and erratic, and our mistakes are quickly forgotten, along with all the times we’ve impressed someone. As Marcus Aurelius stated: “So many who were remembered already forgotten, and those who remembered them long gone.” (5) It destroys authenticity. Care too much about what others think, and you’ll turn into a sheep anxiously following the rest of the flock. If you do as other people want you to do, you’ll be living according to their expectations and ideals. German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche despised the herd mentality that many people carry. He makes a distinction between the Herren- und Sklavenmoral, meaning the master and slave morality. Those at the top are the strong-willed who create values and rules. The many at the bottom, the herd, follow but oppose their oppressors at the same time. But instead of rising to the top, those with a slave morality want others to be at their level, namely, among the other obedient, mediocre, and uniform members of the herd. Once part of the mass, they expect you to be just like them. If you stand out, the herd sees you as evil. If you act in conflict with conventions, you may even be considered dangerous, as people usually fear what’s strange and unknown. Within the pack, conformity is a virtue, and authenticity is a threat. Nietzsche urges his readers to be neither a master nor a slave but transcend this system altogether and become an authentic, self-actualized person. One can only accomplish greatness if one ignores the opinions of the herd and their pre-determined virtues and unapologetically forges one’s own path. (6) Life is too short. A survey of 2,000 British adults called the National Worry Audit revealed that, on average, people in Britain spend about 6,5 years of their lives worrying. Many of these worries concern, directly or indirectly, the opinions of other people. An example. On a daily basis, 28% percent of Brits worry about their appearance, 21% worry about what to wear, and 17% about body odor. The average life expectancy of the British is currently 81 years old, which means that they spend 8 percent of their lives worrying. If they’d simply stop worrying about other people, then they’d have about two additional years to enjoy life or to do something useful. But still, even though 81 years seems quite long, it’s only a fraction of time compared to humanity as a whole, let alone planet Earth. Moreover, many die young, as human life is fragile and can be taken away in the blink of an eye—what a waste of energy to spend this short and vulnerable existence wondering So, the fickleness and shortness of life can be a potent reminder to eliminate this destructive habit. As Seneca wrote: You live as if you were destined to live forever, no thought of your frailty ever enters your head, of how much time has already gone by you take no heed. You squander time as if you drew from a full and abundant supply, though all the while that day which you bestow on some person or thing is perhaps your last. You have all the fears of mortals and all the desires of immortals. (7) You know yourself best. Even though other people can give you valuable outside perspectives concerning your behavior, the person most knowledgeable about you is you. No matter how close we get to each other, our minds remain a private space and often don’t fully resemble what we show to the world. Carl Jung’s model of the psyche differentiates several parts: the persona, the ego, the self, the shadow, and the animus or anima. Of these aspects, the persona is what we show to the world, which is just a thin layer of the self. Or, as Jung put it: “a kind of mask, designed on the one hand to make a definite impression upon others, and on the other to conceal the true nature of the individual.” Some people can be pretty intuitive and see through the cracks of our masks; moreover, they can notice behaviors about us that we aren’t even aware of. But they can never be sure about our true motives, secrets, and hidden personality traits because these are reserved for ourselves only. So, people’s thoughts about us based on what they perceive often don’t align with reality. Therefore, the feedback we get from others can be helpful, but the truth ultimately hides within ourselves. Deep inside, we know what we want, and the more we stay true to that, the more authentic we become, and the less we conform to what other people want us to be. Thank you for watching.

Everything seems to flow in its natural way. As an introduction to the beautiful tradition of Taoism, I would like to present to you the philosophy of blow. The Tao Téqing is a mysterious work of art. There is no consensus on when exactly it was written, and the existence of its author remains questionable. Nevertheless, one thing is indisputable. The depth of this work has left a mark on human history and continues to influence us to this day. Not to mention that the tao tqing is the most translated work in world literature after the bible. The essence of tauist philosophy lies in living in harmony with the toao also called the way. So what is the toao? This is a question we cannot answer precisely and trying to do so is useless. Our understanding of the toao is limited by the boundaries of our perception. What is the towel really? How does it look, feel, smell, or sound? This remains a mystery. Moreover, the tow we speak of is not the true towo according to Lasu. Hence, the famous beginning of the Tao Ting. The Tao that can be described is not the eternal Tao. The name that can be named is not the eternal name. So what is known about the toao? Tauist philosophers repeatedly emphasize that the true toao is a universal force that lies beyond our understanding and cannot be perceived by the senses. And although we can never fully comprehend the true toao the goal is to live in accordance with it which is remarkably similar to the stoic approach to nature. How do we live in harmony with the way? Tauist literature does not offer one specific practical method for this. However, we can find many clues pointing to achieving peace of mind, restraining emotions, humility, and ceasing striving in order to open ourselves to the action of the universe. This peace of mind does not necessarily mean that we sit somewhere with our eyes closed. Tauists note that peace of mind can be combined with action. If we are fully present in the present moment, our actions will happen effortlessly without resistance and with exceptional focus. So much so that it is almost ecstatic. In the tauist works, there's a story about a cook named Ding who engages in his work while in a state of blow. This caught the attention of Lord Hugh, who was amazed at how gracefully the cook butchered the ox. The cook explained his mastery. When I first began butchering oxen, I saw only the ox before me. After 3 years, I no longer saw the whole ox. And now I act with spirit and do not look with my eyes. Perception and understanding have stopped and the spirit moves where it wants. I follow natural structures, cut along large cavities, guide the knife through large openings, following how everything is arranged. Therefore, I never touch even the smallest ligaments or tendons, let alone the main joints. An important part of this story is the condition of the knife the cook uses. He said that good cooks change knives every year because they cut and mediocre cooks change them every month because they chop. However, Cook Ding had used the same knife for 19 years because he applied it with skill and finesse. This story relates to another key teaching of Tauism, the power of softness. By applying force and straining, we can complete a task, but we spend more energy than necessary and risk collateral damage. On the other hand, a person in a state of flow approaches a task wisely, knowing when to act and when to refrain from action. This is not too strong and not too weak an approach. It's the golden mean between anxiety and boredom. The idea of non-action contradicts the western ideal of forcing and ever more persistent work to achieve results. We are encouraged to be ambitious. But in our relentless pursuit, don't we burn ourselves out. We look down on passivity and often confuse it with laziness. But these are different things. When we look at nature, doing nothing turns out to be much more logical than we think. Results do not equal the amount of energy spent. Many of these actions occur naturally and tasks do not require more human intervention than is needed for gentle guidance in the right direction. Isn't it true that many problems resolve themselves? Towoism compares life to a river. The river already has a channel or several channels. And finding ourselves in this river, we can swim against the current, cling to a branch, or let go and float downstream. Most of our lives, we swim against the current and don't even realize it. Our mind believes that it can and should control the environment for survival, which is quite egocentric. Think about it. We don't control processes in the body such as digestion, circulation, or wound healing. We don't control other people. We don't control the future. We don't even control who we fall in love with or whom we find attractive. Everything that is beyond our capabilities simply goes in some direction. Sometimes this direction is set by the mind, but more often by the natural course of things. When we go with the flow, we align with this natural course. This is the path of least resistance. It gives nature a chance to unfold without meeting our opposition. Thus, the towist approach is more about navigating the river than trying to control it. The latter will never work. Another aspect of the river characteristic of Taoism is water itself. The properties of water, softness, and humility symbolize the Tao. Here's a quote from the Tao Ting. The highest good is like water which brings benefit to all things without competing with them. It gathers in unpopular places. Thus, it is close to the towel. Water can be soft, but it overcomes hardness as seen in the erosion of rocks. Water is humble, yet it nourishes everything it passes. This is an incredible life force that literally works miracles, but without any ambition. Water is the softest and most pliable substance. But nothing surpasses water in overcoming the hard and rigid because nothing can compete with it. One thing that disappears and returns only when the mind takes control again is focus on results rather than the task itself. When you are in a state of flow, you forget about results, pressure, anxieties about the future, failures of the past. There is only you and what you are doing right now. You are completely in the present. And the only way to achieve this is to let go. Letting go means stopping swimming against the current, stopping clinging to branches. It means letting go of the need to control, concentrating entirely on this moment and simply living in it without hesitation.

- The Tao Explained E2 Wu Wei Effortless Action: Kind: captions Language: en Wooi is one of the most misunderstood ideas in Taoism. It is often translated as non-action, but it does not mean doing nothing. Wooi means effortless action, [music] acting in a way that fits the moment without force, strain, or resistance. Imagine pushing on a door that will not open. You push harder and harder, wasting energy. Then you realize the door was meant to be pulled. Wooi is about noticing how things naturally work and adjusting yourself to that flow. In nature, nothing struggles to be what it is. Rivers do not force themselves forward. Trees do not rush their growth. Yet everything gets done. When we overthink, rush or try to control outcomes, we create resistance. Wooi teaches us to pause, observe, and respond instead of react. This kind of action is not weak. It is precise. A small movement at the right time can achieve more than constant [music] effort. Living with wooi means letting go of ego-driven action. - TAOISM | The Power of Letting Go: Kind: captions Language: en Mastery of the world is achieved by letting things take their natural course. You can not master the world by changing the natural way. Lao Tzu Our civilization is in a state of ongoing strivings, in which control seems to be the highest virtue. We don’t have to look far to observe this: in the workplace, for example, employees are more and more controlled and supervised, especially now we have the technology to do so. And governments put more effort into tracking their citizens, whether it’s through camera supervision or the proposal of a so-called ‘social credit system’. Ironically, the latter is a Chinese invention, that goes utterly against a philosophy that emerged from the same soil: Taoism. As opposed to a control-obsessed society, Taoism revolves around letting go and going with the flow. At first glance, the act of letting go may seem a form of weakness. But according to the Taoists, by a correct understanding of how the universe works, we can approach life more intelligently, more efficiently, and go with the flow, rather than swimming against it. Therefore, the power of letting go is a form of strength that’s based on sophistication rather than force. The Tao Te Ching, the main Taoist scripture, was written by a mysterious sage named Lao Tzu. There are countless ways in which we can interpret this text. One way is to see it as a guide for a ruler. What characterizes the passages of the Tao Te Ching regarding governance, is that Lao Tzu puts emphasis on ruling by ‘not ruling’, as he compared governing a country with frying a small fish: too much poking spoils the meat. He argued that when a ruler tightens his grip on the people, all kinds of negative side effects will occur. We see that people become distrustful towards one another when the government is too patronizing, and when it’s too intrusive, people become rebellious. But when a leader is unobtrusive and acts with integrity, then people will become whole, as they’re granted the space to naturally evolve. It’s clear that Lao Tzu favors a passive form of governance, which doesn’t just apply to ruling a state, but also to the governance of ourselves. Because letting things go, is key to let nature do the work, which applies to any level. In this video, I’d like to show you several ways in which Taoism shows us the power of letting go. The first one is the art of... (1) Non-doing The Taoist concept of Wu Wei can be explained as ‘effort action’, or the so-called ‘flow state’, but also as ‘non-doing’, or ‘knowing when to act and when not to’.’ When we take a critical look at ourselves, we see that the need for control prevails in many areas of life. We feel the need to control our pets, our children, our gardens, our video games, (in some cases) our partners, and first and foremost: our future. Now, control isn’t always a bad thing. In order to survive, we need to exert our influence on the environment to some extent. Especially self-control can lead us in a positive direction. Without control, human civilization would probably never have occured. But too much of it doesn’t get us anywhere. It seems that we systematically underrate the natural influences that lie at the basis of our daily lives. We can’t control everything, and many things happen when we stop controlling them. Let’s take a tree for example. We can plant it, we can water it, we can add some fertilizer, and make sure it’s exposed to enough sunlight. But any more intervention would only damage the process because we interrupt nature from doing its job. Another example is attraction. The first step to attracting someone is simply showing ourselves, so that the person we want to attract knows that we exist. Then, attraction either happens or not. When the attraction is there, one can easily blow it by taking too much action. Attraction is a natural phenomenon that is beyond our control. It absolutely cannot be enforced. Instead, it has to grow, or erupt spontaneously. And there’s only one way to let the seed of attraction grow into a beautiful tree; which is not intervening, aside from the occasional watering. Silence makes the heart grow fonder. That’s why ‘letting go’ is vital in relationships. Because by letting go, we give space to the forces of the universe to unfold. After a fight, for example. anger naturally erodes. And when trust is breached, one cannot enforce restoration: it has to grow back naturally. So, letting go makes the difference between controlling and allowing. The second one is... (2) Embracing change. The Taoists were very aware that life unfolds in a constant movement between opposites: between high and low, light and dark, yin and yang. There isn’t much we can do about it, and the most efficient way of living is simply moving along with the waves of existence. The flow of life and its transformations are inevitable. Yet, we see so many people cling to their circumstances. In the metaphor of the river stream, they hold on tightly to a branch or rock, afraid to let go, because they want complete control over their position. They simply don’t trust the universe. And the consequence of this is a rigid lifestyle. They see life passing them by, including many opportunities for positive change, and they miss out on a lot of fun. As Lao Tzu wrote in the Tao Te Ching, and I quote: The living are soft and yielding; the dead are rigid and stiff. Living plants are flexible and tender; the dead are brittle and dry. End quote. There are also those who swim against the stream. They’re the biggest energy wasters of them all. Perhaps they see honor and virtue in taking an extremely non-agreeable stance in life. But exercising a constant resistance to how the universe unfolds, isn’t a very efficient way to live, and most likely makes one worn-out and miserable. This non-acceptance of ‘how things are’ is also the cause of people fighting against themselves. Because of certain societal expectations, people engage in a battle against their inherent nature, instead of flowing along with the attributes that nature has given them. We could say: “follow your strength, instead of trying to repair your weakness.” Embracing change also applies to uselessness and usefulness. Taoist philosopher Zhuangzi observed that usefulness depends on the circumstances, as he told about a merchant that tried to sell shirts to a tribe, whose members were covered in tattoos, and always showed them off by walking around shirtless. To them, shirts are useless. But to us, at least most of us, they aren’t useless at all. Usefulness and uselessness are relative and are not to be treated with rigidity. When you live in New York, for example, having a car is less useful, then when you live somewhere in the countryside where the next village is fifty kilometers away. So, we ought to be willing to let go of things that are useless in one situation, and adopt what’s useful instead. That’s how we make change an ally, and not enemy. The third one is... (3) Not focusing on outcomes. Comparable to the Stoics, the Taoists observed that the focus on future outcomes has a negative effect on us. Focusing too much on the future makes us anxious. Our present endeavors become fueled by a desire for an uncontrollable result, and the more we crave that, the less we value the only thing we have, which is the present moment. Zhuangzi goes one step further, by telling us that the more we value something external, the worse we perform in the present. He tells us about an archer that loses his ability to shoot when he focuses too much on the prize. He who is contending for a piece of earthenware puts forth all his skill. If the prize be a buckle of brass, he shoots timorously; if it be for an article of gold, he shoots as if he were blind. The skill of the archer is the same in all the cases; but (in the two latter cases) he is under the influence of solicitude, and looks on the external prize as most important. All who attach importance to what is external show stupidity in themselves. Now, this doesn’t mean that people that want external things are stupid. It means that when our minds are in the future, we paralyze ourselves in the present. This principle lies at the basis of the ‘flow state’ that we see in activities like sports, art, and dancing. When we experience this flow state, we’re so immersed in the task at hand, that we completely forget about the future. It’s like the dance dances itself. The last one for now is... (4) Letting go of excess. In a society in which status is an ultimate concern, everyone wants to be at the top. Not because it’s necessarily the best place to be, but because we’ve collectively decided that high status is preferable and low status is horrible. This also comes with a collective pursuit of the former, and a collective aversion to the latter. But the tallest trees catch the most wind. And when we’re at the top, it takes a tremendous amount of effort to stay there, because everyone wants to take your position. It’s stressful compared to the lower regions, in which one lives more privately, with less competition, less enemies, and, in general, less effort. The other extreme, however, is a place of deprivation. If we deliberately seek the absolute bottom, we become ascetics. Although in a different way, there’s still a strong attachment; the attachment to deprivation. The question we can ask ourselves is: what do we truly need? Zhuangzi observed that a bird that nests in the forest, wants no more than one branch. And that a mouse that drinks from the pond, drinks no more than a bellyful. So, if we aim for what we need, and let go of excess, we prevent possessions from becoming our prison cell, which allows us to travel light. Epicurus observed as well that the basic necessities for life are easy to come by, and that living moderately is the key to happiness. It’s a path that’s easy, and sustainable. As Lao Tzu wrote: “Those who use moderation are already on the path to the Tao.” When we stop striving, we give nature space to unfold. In trusting the universe and accepting that it’s ever-changing lies the opportunity to become loose and supple, instead of rigid and brittle. The power of letting go means that we float along the stream, without grasping for rocks and branches, and that we cut loose dead weight, so we can navigate through life with minimal effort. Thank you for watching.

  2. @jaybradley5462 [1 likes]: Couple of inaccuracies. Alcohol distillation was in Ireland from 1324 (Red Book of Ossary), not 1500 or 1600 in Europe. There's evidence of a common ape ancestor being able to breakdown ethanol in the liver for over 10 million years. Either way, whether it's 40% or 5% abv, it's still ethanol. For example, my lineage, being Celtic/Viking, has been drinking 5-15% alcohol for over 4,500 years. and distilled spirit above 40% for 700 years. While 700 years might not be enough for evolution to adjust, it doesn't need to, as our liver had adjusted to ethanol for many millennia before that. Distilled spirit is just cleaner alcohol without the tannins, histamines, sulfites and residual sugars like beer and wine. So if you drink a like-for-like volume of ethanol, you'll be less sick or hungover from distilled spirits versus beer or wine. Just have to be careful with how much you consume.

「道」和「德」二字各是什麼？合起來是什麼？意義是什麼？請參詳高本衲宏文 何謂道德？。不開玩笑也不是老王賣瓜自賣自誇，這篇文章絕對精確也很重要，你可以拿去比對古今中外碩學宏儒的任何相關論述，找到錯誤高某一定從善如流立即修正。

道者天地運行之至理，德者人我承感之真情也。
道屬天屬地不屬人。以是，道從首從走不從人。故曰：“大道之行也，天下為公”、“人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然”。
德屬人不屬天地。以是，德從人不從天、不從地。故曰：“道生之，德畜之”、“為而不恃，長而不宰，是謂玄德”。
人必無單，因此德從雙人。德又從心。心者念也，在內；行者為也，在外。心乃行之始，行乃心之終，是謂“德行”。行無自了，必有之於人，故行亦從雙人。又，人者心之器也，故德行終不離人。
天地無心，故大道無情，宋儒張載遂曰：“為天地立心”。無心則寡情，寡情則不親，故曰：“太上忘情，天道無親”。
天道無心、寡情、不親，卻有常。常者永也，必也，真也。故天道即常道，常道即常理，常理即真理。
人皆有目，目木成相。人又有心，相成心上是為想。想者念也，念者今心也，今者當下也，俱心之用也。
念有善惡，惡亦從心，故又屬人。人皆有情，情有愛情、感情、真情、友情，卻無惡情，以惡念無情也。日青乃晴，水青則清，人青是倩，心青為情。
德有玄德、恩德、盛德、美德，而無惡德，概惡者非德也。
準此，何謂“道德”？合理之謂道，有情是為德。
理者天地運行之正道，情者人我承感之盛德也。
