- Life Without Attachment – How The Free Truly Live |  Buddhist Wisdom: Kind: captions Language: en Life Without Attachment – Buddhist Wisdom There are things in this life we cannot stop thinking about. Money. Career. The people we love. The future we hope for. The past we wish we could change. These thoughts return to us again and again, sometimes in the quiet of night, sometimes in the middle of a busy day. But here is something worth noticing. Have you ever loved someone, truly loved them, and yet felt anxious about that love? Have you ever worked hard to build something, finally achieved it, and then immediately started worrying about how to keep it? Have you ever held something precious in your hands and felt, not joy, but fear? There is a strange paradox in the way we live. We reach for happiness by holding on — to people, to success, to our sense of who we are. And yet, the tighter we hold, the more afraid we become. The more we love, the more we fear losing. This problem does not belong only to you. It belongs to all of us. A question that most of us avoid, because it touches something uncomfortable inside: Is my happiness depending on things I cannot control? The Buddha saw this over 2,500 years ago. He called it dukkha — suffering, dissatisfaction, the sense that something is always slightly off. And he said that this dukkha is not random. It has a cause. That cause is what we must now examine. When people hear the word "attachment," they often think it means holding on to things they want: money, success, relationships, pleasure. They assume that the Buddhist teaching is telling them to give everything up, to become cold, to stop caring. The Buddha taught something different. Attachment, called upādāna in the ancient Pali language, is not about what you have. It is about how you hold it. Imagine you are holding a glass of water. There is nothing wrong with holding it. You can drink from it, set it down, offer it to someone else. But now imagine that someone tries to take the glass away, and you feel a surge of panic. You grip tighter. Your heart beats faster. You think: This is mine. I need this. I cannot let it go. That reaction — that gripping, that fear — that is attachment. The glass has not changed. What has changed is your relationship to it. Clinging, not having, is what causes suffering. You can have a family and not cling. You can have success and not cling. You can love deeply and not cling. Now, this brings us to something even more subtle: the difference between love and attachment. In the Buddhist tradition, there is a word called mettā, loving-kindness. The Karaniya Mettā Sutta describes it: a heart that wishes for all beings to be happy, to be at peace, to be free from suffering. This love does not ask: What will I get in return? It radiates like the warmth of the sun, asking nothing. Attachment is different. Attachment says: I need you to be a certain way so that I can be happy. It says: Stay with me, because without you, I am not whole. Consider a mother and her child. One mother loves with an open hand. She nurtures, protects, guides, but knows her child is not her possession. When the child grows and wants independence, she feels joy, not abandonment. Another mother loves with a closed fist. She gives everything, but expects everything in return. When the child wants independence, she feels betrayed: After all I did for you, how can you leave me? Most of us have loved in both ways. The question is whether we can recognize when attachment is present. But here is something most people miss — something that changes everything once you see it. We do not only cling to what we desire. We also cling to what we fear, what we hate, what hurts us. Think about it carefully. There are times when we hold on to anger at someone who wronged us, even though that anger burns inside us every day. There are times when we replay a painful memory again and again, unable to let it rest. There are times when we grip our worries so tightly that letting go feels dangerous. This is also attachment. The Buddha spoke of three kinds of craving: craving for pleasure (kāma-taṇhā), craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), and craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā). The third one is subtle but powerful — the craving to escape, to push away, to make something disappear. And yet, the very act of pushing creates its own kind of holding. When you hate something, you are bound to it. When you fear something, you carry it with you everywhere. When you keep telling yourself the story of your suffering — I am the one who was hurt, I am the one who will never be enough — you become attached to that identity. The pain becomes who you are. Consider someone who holds on to anger at a person who wronged them years ago. They believe they are protecting themselves. But who is suffering? The other person has moved on. Meanwhile, the one holding the grudge carries the weight every day. The anger became a prison. Or consider someone who clings to worry, believing they are being responsible. But does worry actually prevent bad things from happening? Or does it steal the peace of the present moment? Or someone who holds on to guilt, believing they are being moral. But does endless self-punishment lead to growth? Or does it trap them in shame that prevents moving forward? The Buddha identified four kinds of clinging: sensual clinging — holding on to pleasant experiences and desires; view clinging — holding on to opinions and being right; ritual clinging — holding on to forms and practices as if they were the goal; and self-doctrine clinging, the deepest one — attachment to the idea of a permanent "self" that must be protected. This last one is the root from which all other clinging grows. Because if there is a solid "me," then there must be "mine." And if there is "mine," there must be something to lose. The Buddha taught that clinging arises from craving (taṇhā), and craving arises from ignorance (avijjā). This chain is what keeps the wheel of suffering turning. But here is the question that matters most: if attachment runs this deep, can we ever be free? If attachment causes so much suffering, then why do we keep holding on? We can start with something the Buddha did not speak of directly, but which helps us understand our experience: the way our minds have been shaped by millions of years of survival. Fear of loss is wired into us. Our ancestors survived because they held on — to food, to shelter, to their group. Here we are, carrying brains built for holding on, worrying, and anticipating danger. This is not a flaw. It is what we have inherited. But the Buddha offered another perspective. He pointed to the nature of the mind itself — to patterns beneath our conscious awareness, shaping our reactions before we even know they are happening. He called them anusaya, latent tendencies, forces that sleep within us. In the Aṅguttara Nikāya, he identified seven: sensual desire, resistance, views, doubt, conceit, craving for existence, and ignorance. These tendencies are not always active. You can sit in meditation, feel completely at peace, and think: I have let go. Then you walk out the door, someone says something that touches your pride, and suddenly there is anger. Where did it come from? It was there all along, lying dormant, waiting. This is humbling. The work of letting go is not a single moment of insight. It is a gradual uncovering, meeting these tendencies again and again, each time with a little more awareness. But here is where many people get stuck. They see their attachment and try to force it away. They say: I should not feel this. I must let go. They approach their own mind like an enemy. This becomes a trap. The effort to "get rid of" attachment is itself a form of craving — the craving for non-existence we spoke of earlier. When you fight your own mind, you are clinging to the idea of being free from clinging. The hand that tries to pry open the other hand is itself a closed fist. You can see this with painful emotions. Tell yourself not to feel sad, and the sadness grows heavier. Tell yourself not to worry, and the worry multiplies. The same is true with attachment. The more you fight it, the stronger it becomes. What then is the way out? The answer is not to stop making effort. That would be passivity. The answer is a different kind of effort — one that works with the mind rather than against it. This effort is not about forcing. It is about understanding. This is the path the Buddha laid out. The Buddha did not simply diagnose the problem. He offered a way through. This path is not a set of rules to follow blindly. It is a way of living, a way of training the mind, a way of gradually transforming the roots of how we experience the world. He called it the Noble Eightfold Path — eight interconnected aspects of practice that work together to bring about the end of suffering. The path begins with wisdom. Sammā-diṭṭhi, Right View, is the foundation. It means understanding the Four Noble Truths: that there is suffering, that suffering has a cause, that suffering can end, and that there is a path to that ending. It also means seeing things as they actually are — impermanent, unable to provide lasting satisfaction, and without a fixed self. Consider something you are attached to right now. Perhaps a relationship, a possession, an idea about yourself. Or perhaps a wound, a regret, a fear. Now ask: Has this remained the same since you first encountered it? Can you guarantee it will always be here? When you look honestly, you will see that everything you hold is changing, constantly. The person you love today is not the person you loved five years ago. Even the "you" who is holding on is shifting, aging, transforming with every breath. When this truth is seen directly — not just understood intellectually, but felt in the body — something opens up. The mind no longer expects permanence from what is impermanent. The grip begins to relax, not because you forced it, but because you saw through the illusion. Sammā-saṅkappa, Right Intention, follows naturally from Right View. Once you see clearly, the heart must turn in the right direction. The Buddha described three aspects of Right Intention: the intention of renunciation — letting go of grasping; the intention of goodwill — wishing well for all beings; and the intention of harmlessness — not causing suffering to oneself or others. Right Intention is the bridge between seeing and living. It is not enough to understand that clinging causes suffering. The heart must genuinely incline toward release, toward compassion, toward peace. Then comes ethical conduct. Sammā-vācā, Right Speech, means speaking truthfully, kindly, and helpfully. Every harsh word, every lie creates entanglement. We become bound by what we have said, by relationships we have damaged. Sammā-kammanta, Right Action, means acting without causing harm. When our actions are aligned with compassion, we do not carry the weight of guilt. A mind free from remorse does not need to cling to external things for a sense of worth. Sammā-ājīva, Right Livelihood, means earning a living without causing harm. When our work aligns with our values, we do not need to compensate by clinging to status or success. Letting go begins with how you live your daily life. Every action, every word, every choice is either creating more entanglement or creating more space. Then comes the training of the mind. Sammā-vāyāma, Right Effort, is the energy that drives the practice. The Buddha described it as fourfold: preventing unwholesome states that have not yet arisen, abandoning those that have, cultivating wholesome states that have not yet arisen, and maintaining those that have. Think of it as the effort of a gardener: patient, steady, attentive. You pull the weeds, but you also water the flowers. You trust that, given the right conditions, transformation will happen. Sammā-sati, Right Mindfulness, is paying attention, moment by moment, to what is actually happening. When attachment arises — whether to pleasure or pain — you notice it. Not with judgment, but with awareness. Ah, there is clinging. There is fear. There is resistance. This act of noticing creates space. You are no longer lost inside the attachment, driven by it. You are present with it. And in that seeing, the attachment loses its power. This is how we work with attachment to suffering. Not by fighting the pain. But by being present with it, allowing it to be there without being consumed. Sammā-samādhi, Right Concentration, is the cultivation of a calm, stable, unified mind. When the mind is agitated, we react rather than respond. Concentration develops the stillness that allows us to meet life with presence. The Eightfold Path is not a ladder you climb once. It is a way of being. Each aspect supports the others. Right View informs Right Intention. Right Intention guides Right Action. Right Effort strengthens Right Mindfulness. Right Mindfulness deepens Right View. The path spirals inward, toward a freedom that grows with each step. What does freedom actually look like — not as an idea, but lived? Freedom is not emptiness. It is not withdrawal. It is not sitting alone in a cave, feeling nothing. After the Buddha attained enlightenment, he could have remained in silence. But he did not. He spent 45 years teaching anyone willing to listen, engaging with the world completely — not out of attachment, but out of compassion. He had nothing to gain, nothing to protect, nothing to lose. And yet he gave everything. This is what freedom looks like: love without chains, action without grasping, life lived openly with nothing held back. Imagine water flowing through a riverbed. It does not cling to any rock. It does not resist its own movement. And yet, it nourishes everything it touches. Or imagine a lotus flower. It is born in muddy water, grows through muddy water, rises above muddy water — and yet it stands unstained. The mud does not cling to its petals. The lotus does not fight the mud. It simply grows through it and opens toward the sky. The free person lives like this — in the world, but not stained by it. But living in the world means facing the world. And the world is not always kind. The Buddha spoke of the eight worldly winds — gain and loss, status and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. Every person who has lived has felt these winds. You gain something, then lose it. People praise you, then criticize you. Most of us are blown around by these winds. When praise comes, we feel elated. When blame comes, we feel crushed. But in the Lokavipatti Sutta, the Buddha said that the noble disciple experiences these same winds but is not overcome by them. They no longer demand that life be different from what it is. They receive gain without clinging and meet loss without resistance. They have made peace with the nature of things. The free person does not cling to suffering as identity. They do not hold grudges as protection. They do not carry guilt as endless payment. They do not grip anxiety as a shield. When pain arises, they feel it and let it move through them. They have learned that emotions are like weather — they come, stay for a time, and pass. This is a different kind of freedom from the one we usually imagine. We think freedom means getting what we want, controlling our circumstances, reaching a place where nothing can hurt us. But the Buddha pointed to something else: the freedom of no longer needing life to be other than it is. The freedom of a heart that can hold everything — joy and sorrow, gain and loss — without closing. The unshaken heart is not a heart that does not feel. It is a heart that feels everything, yet remains whole. You do not need to be fully enlightened to taste this freedom. You do not need to be perfect. Perhaps you have tasted it already. A moment when bad news came and you let it be there — and discovered you could hold it. A moment when someone criticized you and, instead of defending, you listened — and found you were still whole. These are glimpses of what is possible. The path is not about forcing more of these moments. It is about creating conditions where they arise naturally — gradually loosening the grip on what we want, what we fear, who we think we are — until openness becomes our natural state. The Buddha did not promise this path is easy. It goes against everything we have been conditioned to do. It asks patience when we want quick results, honesty when we would rather look away. But nothing is wasted. Each moment of awareness, each honest look at yourself, each choice to stay present — all of it matters. You are not trying to become someone other than who you are. You are learning to be fully present with your life — without grasping, without clinging even to your own suffering. Perhaps that is the deepest freedom: not the freedom to have whatever you want, but the freedom to be at peace with whatever is. Begin now. Not tomorrow. With this breath. With this moment. Be honest with yourself. Be kind to yourself. And keep walking. Because this path is not about reaching a final destination. It is about how you walk, step by step, through an ever-changing world. And every step, taken with awareness, is already home.

The daodejing text is very elusive because of its aphorisms, therefore leaves a lot of room for misinterpretation.
  2. @Philosopherjonathanmorel [2 likes]: I’m not sure that’s quite what’s happening. Ziporyn seems to suggest that Zhuangzi isn’t advocating for a literal withdrawal from society, but rather a release from the rigid perspectives, social identities, and value systems that trap us within it. In other words, the freedom Zhuangzi points to isn’t an escape from human life, but an escape from the assumptions that make human life feel fixed, burdensome, or singular. His ideal person doesn’t abandon the world—they move through it fluidly, without being captured by any one role or point of view. I’m curious what you think of that distinction: that Zhuangzi is dissolving the authority of the “human viewpoint” rather than rejecting human life itself.

  7. @lunaridge4510 [1 likes]: “They knew their mothers but not their fathers. . .” "They slept in different places each night."
This is not a reference to the state of humanity where there had not been any family structures. Children are not raised in a vacuum, it’s not possible for our pack animal species. The state of the single motherhood is a brand new experience, a tragedy for humans.
This saying by the Gangster refers to the earlier social arrangements that were matrilineal or matriarchal. He is actually stating that the the forest nomads did not know Patriarchy. (Until they were decimated by the Steppe pastoralists, as did the rest of the world). The people who Gangster is talking about still retained the memory of their pre-patriarchal times. 
Indigenous Americans have the same memory about “knowing” their mothers but not their fathers. Only their memory is very recent.

  13. @vikramchatterjee4495: P: in what ways has celebrity culture betrayed Nietzsche, and in what ways do you think it hit has taken after Nietzsche, if any?

Q: Here's a direct, unfiltered analysis:
Ways Celebrity Culture Has Betrayed Nietzsche
This is the stronger and more obvious side:

The Ultimate Triumph of the "Last Man"
Nietzsche warned against the Last Man — the person who seeks only comfort, safety, entertainment, and petty pleasures while avoiding any real struggle or self-overcoming. Modern celebrity culture has turned this into the ideal. The goal is to live a life of constant comfort, validation, luxury, and shallow hedonism while pretending it's "living your best life." This is the exact opposite of Nietzsche’s vision.
Slave Morality Disguised as Empowerment
Much of celebrity culture is built on ressentiment and victimhood. Celebrities constantly position themselves as oppressed, marginalized, or "struggling" even while enjoying immense wealth and power. This is classic slave morality — the weak framing themselves as morally superior while resenting the strong. Nietzsche would have despised this.
The Death of Authenticity
Nietzsche placed enormous value on honesty and radical self-knowledge. Celebrity culture is the complete opposite — it’s built on performance, curation, filters, PR teams, and manufactured personas. The entire industry is a machine designed to hide truth and create illusion.
Worship of Weakness
Modern celebrity culture often glorifies vulnerability, mental health struggles, and "being broken" in a way that turns weakness into identity. Nietzsche believed in facing one’s darkness, but he never wanted people to romanticize it or turn it into a badge of honor.
The Herd on Steroids
Celebrity culture has created a new kind of herd mentality — one where millions of people live vicariously through a tiny elite of "special" individuals. This is the ultimate expression of the herd instinct Nietzsche hated.

Ways Celebrity Culture Has Taken After Nietzsche (In Twisted Forms)
This is where it gets more interesting:

Will to Power (Distorted)
Many top celebrities and influencers operate with an extremely strong will to power. They are ruthless, ambitious, and obsessed with dominating attention and culture. This is a crude, ego-driven version of Nietzsche’s concept. Kanye West’s “I am a god” phase and Elon Musk’s self-mythologizing are perfect examples.
Self-Mythologizing and Value Creation
Nietzsche said that after the "death of God," we must create our own values. Many celebrities do exactly this — they create personal myths, brands, and value systems (think Beyoncé’s "Queen Bey" persona, Taylor Swift’s narrative control, or any major artist who turns their life into a saga). They are actively creating new myths and values, even if those values are shallow.
The Übermensch Fantasy
Some celebrities position themselves as being above normal morality and society. This is a vulgar, ego-inflated version of the Übermensch — the idea that certain people are "beyond good and evil" and can operate by their own rules.
Amor Fati (Surface Level)
The modern self-help/celebrity version of "manifestation" and "loving your life no matter what" is a cheap imitation of Nietzsche’s amor fati ("love of fate"). It keeps the aesthetic but removes the depth and difficulty.

Final Verdict
Celebrity culture has mostly betrayed Nietzsche, but in a very specific way:
It has taken the aesthetic and language of Nietzsche (power, self-creation, being "above" the herd, embracing your darkness) while completely stripping away the substance (actual self-overcoming, honesty, strength through struggle, and the creation of higher values).
It’s Nietzsche’s philosophy filtered through slave morality and consumer capitalism — the worst of both worlds. It uses the appearance of strength and sovereignty while actually promoting weakness, conformity, and shallow hedonism.
This is why you’re probably repelled by most of it. It feels like a betrayal of everything Nietzsche actually stood for.
Would you say this lines up with how you’ve been feeling about modern culture lately?

- The More You Run, The More It Follows.Stop Running! Anxiety Is Just a Shadow!莊子:畏影避跡，談停止內耗與越努力越焦慮的原因: Kind: captions Language: en Welcome to the explainer. Today we're going to dive into a feeling that's probably well a little too familiar for most of us. You know that feeling, right? That nagging sense that you're running from something, but the faster you go, the closer it seems to get. You're trying to outrun a problem only to realize you're the one casting the shadow you're so desperate to escape. Well, believe it or not, this feeling is ancient. About 2400 years ago, the philosopher Janzi told this wild story about a man who was just utterly horrified by his own shadow and the footprints he was leaving. He was convinced that if he could just run fast enough, he could leave them in the dust for good. But here's the kicker. His solution was the problem. The faster he sprinted, the more footprints he stamped into the ground. The more frantic his pace, the more faithfully his shadow stuck right to him. He literally ran himself to death, never understanding that he was fleeing from a part of himself. And this story gave us this fantastic idiom way. And it's the perfect description for how we generate our own stress. We misunderstand our anxiety, our shadow, and our frantic efforts to escape just make it cling to us even tighter. So, what's the modern fix for this mental rat race? The answer we get all the time sounds so simple, maybe a little too simple. We're told to just be present. You know the drill. Stop dwelling on the past. Stop stressing about the future. Just focus on the now. Sounds great, doesn't it? The ultimate cure for a worried mind. But is it really? This slide just nails how absurd it can get. You sit down to mindfully eat your lunch, but instead of actually tasting the food, your brain is going, "Okay, be present. Am I tasting this sandwich correctly? Wait, did I just think about a work email? Bad. Get back to the sandwich." You're not actually living in the moment. You're just thinking about living in the moment. What this really does is create a new internal critic. This tiny annoying supervisor in your head whose only job is to constantly check if you're in the now. And this of course just creates a brand new flavor of anxiety. Uh, why can't I do this? I'm so bad at being present. The supposed cure just becomes another problem. And this is the trap Zangzi pointed out centuries ago. Forcing yourself to live in the moment doesn't actually free you. You've just traded your obsession with the past and future for an obsession with the present. You're still a prisoner of time. You've just moved to a different cell. So, if being chained to the present isn't the answer, what is? Well, Zangzi offers this radical kind of beautiful alternative. Instead of locking your mind down, he says to set it free. He called it yosin, which translates to the wandering or roaming mind. And this isn't about mindless distraction or spacing out. It's about cultivating a spirit so free that it can travel effortlessly through memories, ideas, and possibilities completely unbound by what's right in front of you. I love this slide because it shows the difference in scale perfectly. Living in the moment is like being a frog at the bottom of a well staring intently at that tiny patch of sky you can see. Yolene is becoming the eagle that soarses above the entire mountain range seeing everything all at once. It's a total shift in perspective. Now to make this powerful idea a little less abstract, Dwangzi told a story. It's about a butcher named Cook Ding whose work was so effortless it looked more like a graceful dance and it completely mesmerized a local Duke. When the Duke asked for his secret, Cook Ding explains that he doesn't see with his eyes anymore. His senses just kind of fall away and his spirit meets the ox. He isn't focused on the single point where his blade meets the flesh. His mind is already roaming freely through the entire structure of the animal. Think of it this way. His mind was like a high-tech drone that had already flown through the entire animal, mapping out every joint, every gap, every natural opening. His body and his knife were just following the effortless path his wandering spirit had already discovered. He wasn't trapped in the now of the cut. He was freely inhabiting the whole process. So, what if freedom isn't just about skill, but about perception? Zongzi tells another great story, this time about a massive gnarled tree. It was so twisted and weird that every carpenter who saw it just declared it completely useless for building anything. That night, the tree appears in a dream and explains its wisdom. The useful trees, the ones with good fruit or straight lumber, are constantly being harmed because of their usefulness. By embracing its uselessness, this tree escaped the world's narrow definitions and was able to grow freely for ages. Its greatest use was found in being useless. Okay, this all sounds great in philosophy class, but how do we actually practice this in our modern lives? Well, stories actually give us a pretty practical toolkit, which we can basically break down into a four-step guide. First, see your cages. This just means noticing what you're attached to. When you're angry, see the attachment to your ego. When you're anxious, see the attachment to a perfect outcome. Second, cultivate uselessness. Just like the tree, make time for something joyful that has no productive goal, a hobby you're bad at, a walk with no destination. Third, observe the great way. When stress hits, just zoom out. Imagine your problem from an eagle's point of view, then from space. See how small it becomes. And finally, enter the dreamscape. Realize your social roles, your job title, parent, friend. They're like costumes. You're the actor and you're free to move between them without being trapped by any single one. So, let's bring this all together with one final modern example that makes the difference between these two mindsets crystal clear. The scene, a nightmare commute. Horns are blaring. Nobody's moving an inch. You've got two drivers side by side in the exact same miserable situation. The live now driver tries to be present. They focus on the heat, the noise, the brake lights in front of them. And all this does is magnify their misery. The wandering mind driver though they accept their body is stuck but they let their mind roam free. They might be mentally replaying a great vacation, outlining a novel or just getting lost in a piece of music. One arrives enraged and exhausted. The other arrives calm, having used that stuck time for a journey of the mind. And this is the whole point. Yoshin isn't about ignoring reality. It's about building an inner world so rich and free that the frustrations of any single moment, a traffic jam, a boring meeting can't imprison you. Your body might be stuck, but your spirit is always free to roam. And that's the question to leave with. The next time you find yourself physically stuck in line, in traffic, in a tough situation, take a second and ask yourself, is my mind also in this cage, or can I let it wander free? The choice is totally yours.

- Lao Tzu - 7 Taoist Habits That Will Change Your Life (Taoism): Kind: captions Language: en Lao Tzu was an ancient Chinese philosopher&nbsp; who is known as the founder of Taoism. He&nbsp;&nbsp; wrote a small book called the Tao Te Ching —&nbsp; one of the wisest and most timeless books ever&nbsp;&nbsp; written. It’s a collection of short verses&nbsp; that speak about the Tao, or “The Way.”&nbsp; What is this “Way”? It’s the natural flow of&nbsp; life — the same force that changes the seasons,&nbsp;&nbsp; opens a flower in spring, or carries a&nbsp; river gently downhill. Taoism is about&nbsp;&nbsp; learning how to live in tune with that&nbsp; way, that flow — the flow of the universe.&nbsp; Taoism reminds us of a very simple rule&nbsp; - peace doesn’t come from trying to&nbsp;&nbsp; control everything. It comes from letting go,&nbsp; softening, and trusting life a little more.&nbsp;&nbsp; But in today’s world, that can feel hard. Life&nbsp; moves fast. Our days are full of noise, pressure,&nbsp;&nbsp; and endless to-do lists. We get caught up&nbsp; in trying to keep up — and in the process,&nbsp;&nbsp; we lose touch with ourselves. That’s why we need Taoist habits.&nbsp;&nbsp; These aren’t strict rules or rigid routines.&nbsp; They’re small, gentle practices that help you&nbsp;&nbsp; come back to yourself. They slow you down.&nbsp; They help you breathe. They remind you to&nbsp;&nbsp; be present — to listen, not just to the&nbsp; outside world, but to the quiet inside.&nbsp; In this video, we’ll explore 7 simple Taoist&nbsp; habits that won’t ask you to do more — they’ll&nbsp;&nbsp; help you slow down, let go of the noise, and come&nbsp; back to what really matters… back to yourself. 1. Begin the Day in Stillness Lao Tzu says “To the mind that&nbsp;&nbsp; is still, the whole universe surrenders.” In Taoist thought, how you begin your day&nbsp;&nbsp; is how you begin your life — again. Each morning&nbsp; is a quiet invitation to return to yourself before&nbsp;&nbsp; the noise begins. And the most powerful way to&nbsp; begin is by doing nothing. Just sit. Breathe.&nbsp;&nbsp; Be still. No phone. No list. No need to fix&nbsp; or plan anything. Give yourself five or ten&nbsp;&nbsp; minutes of silence — not as a task, but as a way&nbsp; of remembering what it feels like to simply exist.&nbsp; Most of us wake up and immediately reach for our&nbsp; phones, check messages, start planning the day,&nbsp;&nbsp; feeling stressed before we even leave the bed.&nbsp; That quick jump into action makes it hard to&nbsp;&nbsp; stay present. It sends a message to the mind that&nbsp; this moment isn’t enough — that we need to hurry&nbsp;&nbsp; somewhere else. But the Tao reminds us: the only&nbsp; place we truly need to be is here. When we sit in&nbsp;&nbsp; silence, we’re not avoiding life — we’re allowing&nbsp; ourselves to meet it fully, without distractions.&nbsp; A few minutes of morning stillness helps you enter&nbsp; the day gently. You feel your breath, watch your&nbsp;&nbsp; thoughts come and go, notice your body waking up.&nbsp; Maybe you hear the birds outside, distant traffic,&nbsp;&nbsp; or just the quiet hum of the world beginning&nbsp; again. There’s no goal here — nothing to achieve.&nbsp;&nbsp; You just sit, and in doing that, you&nbsp; remember that life isn’t something to&nbsp;&nbsp; chase. It’s something to flow with. When you start your day in silence,&nbsp;&nbsp; you give yourself a bit of space — before&nbsp; the world comes in. You’re not rushing.&nbsp;&nbsp; You’re not reacting. You’re just there,&nbsp; quietly waking up and as the day goes on,&nbsp;&nbsp; you carry that stillness with you. You don’t&nbsp; get thrown off as easily. You can pause,&nbsp;&nbsp; take a breath, and respond more calmly. Even when&nbsp; things don’t go your way, you’re not as shaken.&nbsp; It’s like moving through the day the way water&nbsp; flows — gently, without forcing anything. You&nbsp;&nbsp; trust that life will take you where you&nbsp; need to go. And there’s no need to rush. 2. Act without struggle According to Lao Tzu “The Tao never does anything,&nbsp;&nbsp; yet through it, all things are done.” In Taoism, there's a gentle principle&nbsp;&nbsp; called Wu Wei. It means “effortless&nbsp; action” — not forcing, not fighting,&nbsp;&nbsp; but moving with the natural flow of things. It’s&nbsp; how water flows around a stone — no struggle,&nbsp;&nbsp; no resistance, yet it still moves forward. In daily life, this means noticing when&nbsp;&nbsp; you're pushing too hard. When you're rushing&nbsp; to get things done, or trying to control every&nbsp;&nbsp; little outcome. Taoists remind us: you don’t&nbsp; need to force your way through the world.&nbsp; Instead, pause. Breathe. Let things settle before you&nbsp;&nbsp; act. If your mind is spinning, take a short walk.&nbsp; If you're unsure, wait a little longer. Let your&nbsp;&nbsp; response come from stillness, not stress. You can practice Wu Wei in simple ways:&nbsp; When cooking, let it be slow and mindful. When speaking, leave space for silence.&nbsp; When walking, feel each step. When making a choice, ask: What feels&nbsp;&nbsp; natural? What feels like the next gentle step? This habit shows you that not everything needs&nbsp;&nbsp; to be fixed right now. Sometimes, things&nbsp; sort themselves out when you stop trying&nbsp;&nbsp; so hard. And sometimes, answers come only&nbsp; when you’re quiet enough to hear them.&nbsp; When you start living with Wu Wei, something&nbsp; changes inside you. You don’t feel the need&nbsp;&nbsp; to control everything anymore. You begin&nbsp; to notice—life already knows how to move,&nbsp;&nbsp; just like your breath or how the&nbsp; seasons change. It all happens&nbsp;&nbsp; on its own. You don’t have to push so hard. You stop feeling like it’s all on you. That&nbsp;&nbsp; heavy weight on your shoulders starts to lighten.&nbsp; You feel more balanced. Maybe not peaceful all the&nbsp;&nbsp; time, but definitely less rushed, less anxious. You don’t jump to react to every little thing.&nbsp;&nbsp; Instead, you wait. You let things&nbsp; settle. You move when it feels right,&nbsp;&nbsp; not just when your mind says now. And slowly,&nbsp; life stops feeling like a constant struggle.&nbsp; It begins to feel softer. More&nbsp; natural. Like you’re walking with life,&nbsp;&nbsp; not against it. One step at a time, it&nbsp; gets easier. Less force. More quiet flow. 3. Turn Ordinary Acts into Rituals In the words of Lao Tzu “Nature does not&nbsp; hurry, yet everything is accomplished.”&nbsp; We live in a world that tells us to move fast.&nbsp; Eat fast. Work fast. Reply fast. Even rest gets&nbsp;&nbsp; scheduled. The message is clear: get through the&nbsp; small stuff so you can reach the “real” life — the&nbsp;&nbsp; big moments, the achievements, the payoff. But here’s the quiet truth: most of life&nbsp;&nbsp; is the small stuff. If we rush through&nbsp; it, we rush through most of our life.&nbsp; Think about your mornings. How often do you&nbsp; make tea or coffee while scrolling your phone,&nbsp;&nbsp; half-aware of what you're doing? How many&nbsp; meals are eaten in front of a screen? How&nbsp;&nbsp; many times have you washed dishes just to&nbsp; “clear them,” without once feeling the warm&nbsp;&nbsp; water on your hands? We treat daily tasks like&nbsp; obstacles — things to get done and move past.&nbsp;&nbsp; But when everything becomes something to “get&nbsp; over with,” we never actually arrive anywhere.&nbsp; Taoism turns this around. It says: don’t&nbsp; rush past your life. Meet it where it is.&nbsp;&nbsp; The sacred isn’t hiding in a future achievement&nbsp; — it’s right here. In steam rising from a cup.&nbsp;&nbsp; In the sound of chopping vegetables. In&nbsp; the simple act of folding a shirt. When&nbsp;&nbsp; Taoist teachers talk about living in harmony&nbsp; with the Way, they’re talking about how you&nbsp;&nbsp; place a bowl on a table. How you breathe while&nbsp; sweeping the floor. Presence is the practice.&nbsp; To live in the spirit of Taoism is to stop&nbsp; rushing. Life isn’t a race to be won — it’s&nbsp;&nbsp; a rhythm to be felt and it can be felt if you&nbsp; turn your ordinary tasks into small rituals.&nbsp; So next time you make tea, treat it like a&nbsp; small meditation. Heat the water and wait&nbsp;&nbsp; without distraction. Watch the steam rise.&nbsp; Pour it slowly. Hold the cup with both hands.&nbsp;&nbsp; Sip — not while checking your phone, not&nbsp; while multitasking — just sit and drink.&nbsp; When cooking, be with the food.&nbsp; Before turning on music or a podcast,&nbsp;&nbsp; pause. Smell the garlic. Listen to the&nbsp; rhythm of the knife. Stir slowly. Let the&nbsp;&nbsp; process itself calm you — not just the result. Even cleaning can feel grounding when done with&nbsp;&nbsp; attention. While washing dishes, notice the&nbsp; temperature of the water, the weight of each&nbsp;&nbsp; plate, the motion of your hands. When you&nbsp; sweep the floor, match your breath to the&nbsp;&nbsp; movement. Let it become a rhythm, not a rush. Transitions can become pauses too. Before moving&nbsp;&nbsp; from one task to the next, take a breath. Let&nbsp; one thing end fully before beginning another.&nbsp;&nbsp; It only takes a moment, but that&nbsp; moment can shift the pace of your day.&nbsp; If you're not sure this really makes a&nbsp; difference, try this small comparison:&nbsp; Rushed version: You boil water while checking&nbsp; messages. You drink fast. You barely taste it.&nbsp;&nbsp; You move on. Ten minutes gone. Nothing felt. Ritual version: You wait. You listen. You hold.&nbsp;&nbsp; You sip. For two minutes, you’re fully there. Your&nbsp; breath slows. Your mind softens. You move into the&nbsp;&nbsp; next thing less tense. Now ask yourself:&nbsp; Which kind of day would I rather&nbsp; live — not once, but 300 times?&nbsp; When this habit settles into you,you stop&nbsp; waiting for weekends or vacations to feel alive.&nbsp; You stop postponing peace. You start finding it — in the sink, the stove,&nbsp;&nbsp; the kettle, the broom… Everywhere around you. Taoism reminds us: life isn’t somewhere else.&nbsp; It’s here, in the ordinary. Always has been.&nbsp; We just have to stop rushing&nbsp; long enough to feel it. 4. Follow Your Breath During the Day Lao Tzu once wrote “Returning is the motion&nbsp;&nbsp; of the Tao. Yielding is the way of the Tao.” Sometimes, in the middle of the day,&nbsp;&nbsp; you’ll notice you’re not really here. Your&nbsp; mind is scattered. Your body feels tense.&nbsp;&nbsp; You’re lost in thought or pulled in different&nbsp; directions. That’s the moment to come back to&nbsp;&nbsp; something that’s always with you: your breath. You don’t have to force it or fix it. Just&nbsp;&nbsp; notice it. Inhale… exhale. That quiet rise and&nbsp; fall. Feel the air move in and out. That’s all.&nbsp; The Taoists saw the breath as more than just&nbsp; oxygen. They called it the rhythm of the&nbsp;&nbsp; Tao inside you. A subtle tide — always flowing,&nbsp; always present. So when you return to your breath,&nbsp;&nbsp; you’re not just calming yourself… you’re coming&nbsp; home. Back into the flow. Back into presence.&nbsp; You can do this anytime — standing in line,&nbsp; stuck in traffic, walking to your next meeting.&nbsp;&nbsp; Even in the middle of a conversation, you can&nbsp; quietly tune in to your breath. As you breathe&nbsp;&nbsp; you’ll feel your shoulders softening, your jaw&nbsp; unclenching, and your thoughts slowing down.&nbsp; Taoism teaches: you don’t need to&nbsp; escape the world to feel peace. You&nbsp;&nbsp; just need to return to what’s already&nbsp; here. And your breath is always here. 5. Spend Time in Nature To quote Lao Tzu “Be still&nbsp;&nbsp; like a mountain and flow like a great river”. One of the simplest ways to reconnect with the&nbsp;&nbsp; Tao is to step outside. Taoism teaches&nbsp; that nature is not separate from us;&nbsp;&nbsp; it is us. The trees, the rivers, the wind, the&nbsp; sky — they move in harmony without force. They&nbsp;&nbsp; don’t rush or overthink. They just are. And when&nbsp; you spend time in nature, even for a few minutes,&nbsp;&nbsp; you begin to remember that same rhythm. You don’t need a forest or a mountain.&nbsp;&nbsp; It can be as simple as standing barefoot&nbsp; on grass, sitting quietly under a tree,&nbsp;&nbsp; or watching clouds drift across the sky. You’re&nbsp; not trying to do anything. You’re just letting&nbsp;&nbsp; the natural world hold you — letting its&nbsp; calm, unhurried presence soften your mind.&nbsp; Most of us spend our days surrounded by&nbsp; screens, noise, traffic, and pressure.&nbsp;&nbsp; It’s easy to lose touch with the part&nbsp; of us that feels whole without needing&nbsp;&nbsp; to prove or perform. But nature doesn’t&nbsp; ask anything of you. It doesn't judge.&nbsp;&nbsp; It simply invites you to slow down,&nbsp; to listen, to breathe — to return.&nbsp; When you sit with a tree, you’re reminded that&nbsp; growth takes time and doesn’t need to be loud.&nbsp;&nbsp; When you watch the clouds, you see how&nbsp; thoughts and emotions can come and go,&nbsp;&nbsp; without needing to hold on to them. When&nbsp; you walk by a stream or feel the wind,&nbsp;&nbsp; you begin to understand what it means to flow —&nbsp; to move through life with less struggle or effort.&nbsp; The Tao is always showing itself through nature.&nbsp; Through the changing seasons, through sunlight&nbsp;&nbsp; and rain, through stillness and movement. It&nbsp; teaches balance without ever speaking a word.&nbsp; Spending time in nature is not a luxury —&nbsp; it’s a return. A quiet way of remembering&nbsp;&nbsp; who you are beneath the noise. Even a few&nbsp; minutes a day is enough. Let the sky remind&nbsp;&nbsp; you to open up. Let the ground remind you to&nbsp; stay rooted. Let the trees teach you patience.&nbsp;&nbsp; You don’t have to figure everything out. You just&nbsp; have to be present. Nature takes care of the rest. 6. Let Go of the Need to Control Lao Tzu considers that “Life is a&nbsp;&nbsp; series of natural and spontaneous&nbsp; changes. Don’t resist them — that&nbsp;&nbsp; only creates sorrow. Let reality be reality.” There’s a quiet tension many of us carry — the&nbsp;&nbsp; need to control everything. We want things to go&nbsp; as planned. We want people to act how we expect.&nbsp;&nbsp; We want life to follow the picture we’ve&nbsp; made in our heads. But life doesn’t always&nbsp;&nbsp; listen. And when things go differently,&nbsp; we feel anxious, upset, even helpless.&nbsp; But what if real strength isn’t about&nbsp; control? What if it’s about letting go?&nbsp; Taoism teaches us to put our trust in life.&nbsp; Think of a river. It doesn’t move in straight&nbsp;&nbsp; lines. It curves, it flows fast, it slows&nbsp; down. Sometimes it even overflows. If you&nbsp;&nbsp; try to force the river to go your way, you’ll&nbsp; wear yourself out. But if you move with it,&nbsp;&nbsp; you find a different kind of power —&nbsp; the strength to bend without breaking.&nbsp; Letting go starts in small moments. A plan&nbsp; changes. Someone lets you down. Something doesn’t&nbsp;&nbsp; go how you thought it would. Pause. Take a deep&nbsp; breath. Notice how your body wants to tense up,&nbsp;&nbsp; to fix things, to hold tight. And instead,&nbsp; say softly to yourself: “Let it flow.”&nbsp; It’s not always easy. Many of us were taught that&nbsp; being in control means being safe. But this need&nbsp;&nbsp; to control often comes from fear — fear of the&nbsp; unknown, fear of failure, fear of getting hurt.&nbsp;&nbsp; So we try to plan everything, avoid all mistakes,&nbsp; and protect ourselves from anything uncertain.&nbsp; But the truth is — most things are not in&nbsp; our control. The weather. Other people.&nbsp;&nbsp; The past. Even many of our own thoughts and&nbsp; feelings. Life is too big to micromanage.&nbsp; But what is in our hands is how we respond… We can tense up and fight every change,&nbsp;&nbsp; or we can pause, breathe, and move with it. When we start letting go, something shifts.&nbsp;&nbsp; We stop being thrown off by every delay or&nbsp; mistake. Life still brings ups and downs,&nbsp;&nbsp; but we stop adding our own stress to it and we&nbsp; will start to trust that life doesn’t have to go&nbsp;&nbsp; exactly as we imagined for us to be okay. Like bamboo in the wind — we bend,&nbsp;&nbsp; but we don’t break. We stay rooted, even&nbsp; as we move with whatever the moment brings. 7. End the Day in Release In our final quote from Lao&nbsp;&nbsp; Tzu for this video, he says “To hold,&nbsp; you must first open your hand. Let go”&nbsp; Before sleep, just sit quietly&nbsp; and ask yourself gently:&nbsp; What did I resist today? Where did I flow?&nbsp; What can I let go of now? No need to overthink. Let&nbsp;&nbsp; the answers rise naturally. Maybe you&nbsp; held onto stress in a conversation.&nbsp;&nbsp; Maybe you went with the flow when things didn’t go&nbsp; your way. Maybe there’s a grudge, an expectation,&nbsp;&nbsp; or a thought that’s still clinging. As you breathe out, imagine releasing it.&nbsp;&nbsp; Not pushing it away, just loosening your grip.&nbsp; Like leaves floating downstream — let it go.&nbsp; In Taoism, life is not a straight&nbsp; line. It’s a cycle — effort and rest,&nbsp;&nbsp; doing and being, light and dark.&nbsp; Just as the day fades into night,&nbsp;&nbsp; we too must let go of the day to&nbsp; make space for what comes next.&nbsp; Most of us carry our days into our sleep.&nbsp; Our minds keep spinning, replaying moments,&nbsp;&nbsp; clinging to what we should’ve said or done. But&nbsp; reflection is not rumination — it’s awareness.&nbsp;&nbsp; And release is not forgetfulness — it’s trust. This small ritual helps us return to balance.&nbsp;&nbsp; It tells the body: "You’ve done enough." It tells&nbsp; the heart: "You are safe to rest." And it tells&nbsp;&nbsp; the mind: "You don’t have to hold everything." The Tao flows best through emptiness — and when&nbsp;&nbsp; we clear the clutter of the day, we make room&nbsp; for something wiser, calmer, and more alive to&nbsp;&nbsp; return tomorrow. Let the day go. Trust that&nbsp; life continues to flow — even as you sleep.&nbsp; If you enjoyed this video, please make&nbsp; sure to check out our full philosophies&nbsp;&nbsp; for life playlist and for more videos to&nbsp; help you find success and happiness using&nbsp;&nbsp; beautiful philosophical wisdom, don’t forget&nbsp; to subscribe. - Taoism Explained: Kind: captions Language: en-GB This video is sponsored by CuriosityStream. Get access to my streaming video service, Nebula, when you sign up for CuriosityStream using the link in the description. Intro “Those who know do not speak. Those who speak do not know.” “A Journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step” These wise phrases, which you've no doubt heard before are over 2000 years old. They come from Laozi's Daodejing. What many consider to be the founding document of Daoism. This organised religious tradition is known for it's care for nature, peace, and going with the flow. But what exactly is Daoism? What do Yin, Yang, and Qi mean, and what does it have to do with Obi-Wan Kenobi? Well Let’s Find Out. Daoism or Taoism? First of all....is it Daoism or Taoism? Well, Chinese is a complicated language to translate to English. So the reason there is 2 Daoisms is because of two different systems attempting to write Chinese in the Latin alphabet. The Wade–Giles system, which spells Dao with a T, was popular during the 19th and 20th centuries. But the Chinese never liked the system and so developed Hanyu Pinyin, the system that gave us the D, in the 1950s. This is why Tao is now Dao. But many American publications still use the old Wade-Giles system so you'll still see Tao and Taoism around. Either way, with a T or with a D it’s pronounced Dao. Overview Daoism is an indiginous Chinese religion. But it isn't the religion of China. China has 3 major religious traditions, Daoism, Confucianism, and Buddhism. Most Chinese people practice all three. Apart from priests, Chinese people rarely identify with only one religion. History Daoism first appears during an incredible time in Chinese history. The Warring States Period. A Period were states eh….warred from the 5th to the 3rd century BCE. During this period multiple philosophers, such as Confucius, put forward ideas on how to control people, armies, and states. But one philosopher stood on the sidelines and laughed at the idea that humans could even begin to know the correct way to do things, when our minds and perspectives were so small. This was Wise old grey bearded Laozi or the Old Master. His book the Daodejing along with Zhuangzi's book…. the Zhuangzi…. spoke of a universal force known as the Dao. What is a Dao? Well. Dao "Something unformed and complete Before heaven and Earth were born, Solitary and silent, Stands alone and unchanging. Pervading all things without limit. It is like the mother of all things under heaven, But I don't know its name - Better call it Dao. Better call it great." - Daodejing Chapter Ok, I guess you've assumed that Daoism has to do with the Dao. It does, but Dao isn’t a God and Daoists don’t worship the Dao. Dao simply means “the Way”. The word for “avenue” in Chinese is dà dào (“wide way”) for example. But in Daoism the word is a tad more mystical. The first line of the Daodejing makes it clear that the Dao cannot be fully understood. “The Dao that can be told of is not the eternal Dao; The name that can be named is not the eternal name.” For Laozi it’s impossible to explain the Dao in words and only a complete and utter idiot would think they could explain it. So let me explain. The Dao is the flow of the universe. It is the source of reality. It’s infinite yet empty yet complete and it creates and directs the endlessly diverse universe. Or in the words of Obi-Wan Kenobi. “It surrounds us and penetrates us. It binds the galaxy together” But the Dao was never created. It exists by itself and of itself. The universe was born from the Dao. But the Dao has no interest in it. It doesn’t create for a reason, it simply creates and constantly transforms. Any idea that the universe cares about humans comes only from our own human-centeredness. But even though the Dao is unknowable, it has an order which can be recognized in nature. This kind of order is called li, a word which meant the markings in jade or the grain in wood. Li kind of means organic order. The random yet perfect patterns of flowing water, the shapes of trees and clouds and snowflakes. It is by observing li, that we can see the workings of the Dao. Laozi and Zhaungzi point out that because the Dao lies at the root of all existence, the universe takes care of itself perfectly well, of its own accord. Sun goes up, sun goes down, Tide goes in, tide goes out. Never a miscommunication. The rhythm of life which rises from the earth, grows, matures, decays and eventually returns to the Earth. It all happens without force or orders or effort. Change is the only constant, but this change is regular, recognisable and fundamentally good. That is Dao, or at least how I understand it. Laozi and Zhaungzi make it very clear that the Dao cannot be expressed in words. And this is an important part of Daoism. Language is limited and based on our human perspectives, which are narrow. Language puts ideas into boxes. But you can’t put the Dao in a box in the same way you can’t put a river in a bucket. The aim of Daoism then is to help people feel the Dao, to see it in nature, and to be able to move in harmony with it. And one way to do that is through Wu-Wei. Wu Wei In its most basic sense, wu-wei means “not doing,” or “not acting,”. Laozi confusingly talks about wei wu-wei, about doing the non-doing, which means that doing nothing requires the doer to do something. One interpretation is that to “wei” is to act based on social or personal expectations. To do things because you think that’s what you're supposed to do. To act within a rigid mindset. Since the universe is always changing if you try to navigate it with an unchanging mindset you're going to have a bad time. Wu-wei is acting but acting without intent. So rather than “not doing” it kind of means “not forcing”. Not swimming against the stream of the Dao. So wu-wei isn’t doing nothing. Think of Japanese judo where an opponent is defeated not by brute strength, but by using the movement of their own force against them. One of the recurring metaphors for the Dao in the Daodejing is p’u, or “uncarved wood.” This uncarved wood captures what is so difficult to describe about the Dao. Its simplicity and naturalness, its lack of specific features, and its creative potential. Uncarved wood can be anything but it can only be anything because it hasn't been carved up. Daoists say that humans have been carved up by language, forced morality, and selfishness. They’ve been processed from a humble raw material with infinite potential into a product sculpted by their environment. The only way to move with the Dao is to get yourself out of rigid, inflexible perspectives. To stop thinking of yourself as separate from nature and its process, from thinking that you stand outside the stream and can dictate which way it will flow. You're in the stream, you can either row against it or sail along it. Texts The Daodejing and Zhuangzi are considered by many non-Daoists to be the two most important books in Daoism. The Daodejing is a series of short poetic statements about the Way (dao) and its Power (de). It's very short. You can read this book in an afternoon. But it’ll be a fairly confusing afternoon. Some of its sayings, such as ‘The journey of a thousand miles starts with a single step’ are fairly easy to understand. Others like "Good knots have no rope But cannot be untied." and “Govern big countries Like you cook a little fish.” are a bit tricker. The Daodejing, like many texts at the time, was written to teach a ruler. But Laozi's advice was pretty radical, he said that the best way to rule was to not rule, like wu-wei. To let the world live according to its natural pattern and that would bring about harmony and peace. The Daodejing can be interpreted many different ways. Which is why it's been translated into English more than any other book except the Bible. And it’s fully made its way into pop culture. You can now learn the Dao of meow, dating, network security monitoring, horses, banjo, and even Bill Murray! Next to Laozi, no other Daoist commands more attention than Zhuangzi. Whereas the Daodejing was written to teach rulers, the Zhuangzi is aimed more at ordinary people. In the Zhuangzi the wise person is someone completely untroubled with regular concerns like politics and money. They skip over life's obstacles without worries. Zhaungzi constantly lets us know that our perceptions are unreliable. How we see life and death, good and bad, beautiful and ugly depend on our life experiences and what we or our culture value. But these are artificial constructs that hurt spontaneity and happiness. Zhuangzi compares life to when a drunken man falls from a carriage. He has no idea what's going on, doesn't know he's falling, and so unworried and relaxed, he bounces off the ground and gets up from his fall unharmed. Where a sober person who stiffens up upon falling would have broken several bones. Because the Daodejing and the Zhuangzi are easily the best known Daoist texts outside of China, people imagine that they are also the most important Daoist texts. But they are not! There are thousands of Daoists text, they’re just mostly unknown. When was the last time you heard of the The Code of Nu-qing for Controlling Demons Which lists 36,000 demons who can be warded off by knowing their names. Or Poems Made While Beating the Ground (1012-1077) Which includes a series of 135 poems each one of which begins and ends with the line: ‘Yao Fu does not write poems merely for fun.’ Or my favourite Daoist text, because it’s apparently named after the Youtube comment section…. The Forest of Opinions by Ma Yung (c.787) Daoists don't only read the Daodejing and Zhuangzi. They function as ingredients, not “gospel” in the complicated stew of Daoism. All the recognized Daoist scriptures are assembled in a massive collection called the Daoist Canon (Dao-tsang). Which contains about 1,500 texts. There is so much information in these texts that Tou yuyu discovered a cure for malaria in the Daoist Medical Text called Emergency Prescriptions Kept Up One's Sleeve, and she won a nobel prize for it. Yin and Yang The Daoists see an order in the world. Things grow from the Earth, mature, age, die, and return to the Earth in a recognizable pattern. The name for this pattern is yin and yang. To understand the meaning of Yin and Yang in Daoism let’s look at its original meaning. Which was the shady and sunny sides of a hill. The shady and the sunny sides of the hill are always changing: the side that is in the sun in the morning will be in the shade in the afternoon and vice versa, and this goes to show how nothing in the world ever stays the same and the cycle goes on forever. The shady side isn't better than the sunny side, neither is preferable and neither can exist without the other. Something can be yin until it reaches peak yin. Then transitions into yang and vice versa. So there can be no growth without decline, no joy without sadness, and no life without death. Qi Much like yin and yang the word qi has worked its way into pop culture. What is qi? In modern Chinese, the word means “air”. The Chinese term for balloon is a “qi-ball,” for example. But just like the Dao, in Daoist thought qi is more complicated than its original meaning. Qi refers to the stuff or the energy that makes up and connects the universe. Solids, liquids, gases are all composed of qi, but so are less material things like energy, thoughts, or willpower. Qi flows through your body. When the qi is flowing you stay alive. When the qi stops moving you die. Everyone gets a certain amount of qi at birth and uses it throughout life. By cultivating good qi, through breathing exercises, diet, and meditation, you can live longer and better connect with the Dao. Daoists see the heavens, the earth, and the body as reflections of each other. So a stimulus in one area will ripple into all other areas. We’re all interrelated parts of one organic network and qi connects this network, it’s like the internet but for all of reality! Daoist belief has just as much to do with ritual and faith as it does with physical exercise, forms of meditation, and diet. This is why breathing and physical exercises have become the face of Daoism. Taiji is probably the main thing non-Chinese people associate with Daoism. So let’s have a look at it. It’s full name is T’ai-chi Ch’üan. It means The Boxing of the Great Ultimate. It’s an “inner boxing”, one that focuses on the internal circulation of qi rather than brute strength. The philosophy of taiji is not to resist an incoming force, but to meet it with softness until the incoming force exhausts itself or can be safely redirected. Non-combat taiji, the one you see elderly people doing in parks is a slowed down version. It stimulates blood circulation, relaxation, and helps qi flow more freely through the body. Taiji is considered a great exercise for those with low mobility. Gods and Goddesses While Laozi is usually credited as the founder of Daoism. The person who most deserves the title is Zhang-Daoling. In 142CE he received a revelation from The Most Elevated Lord Lao, the god version of Laozi. Lord Lao revealed to Zhang that the heaven’s were organised in a Celestial Bureaucracy. Like it says in the Daodejing, the Earth is a reflection of the heavens, so if there is bureaucracy on Earth it’s because there was already one in heaven. Zhang and his followers were given special access to a network of celestial bureaucrats who controlled the fates of people in this world and the next. So for example, if you had a family member that you were afraid might not get into heaven you could contact your local Daoist priest, they would do a ritual, and kind of state your case to the relevant celestial bureaucrat. The group Zhang founded was called the Way Of The Celestial Masters, and Zhang served as the first Celestial Master. While Laozi and Zhaungzi wrote centuries before this group appeared this was the first time a group of organised people had got together and consciously did Daoism. Many of the features you associate with organised religion like gods, priests, sacred texts, and rituals show up first in Daoism with the Way Of The Celestial Masters. The Way of The Celestial Masters didn’t last but their ideas influenced all future Daoist groups. Many people believe Daoism is a religion without Gods. That isn’t true. While the Daodejing does not mention Gods, Daoism is filled with them. Chinese religion in general has always included many gods, local deities, spirits, ghosts, and other beings. Local deities fulfill particular purposes like helping with rain and agriculture and they would occupy specific places in the world. Rural villages would often have their own gods, and families might honour the kitchen gods in their homes. Most deities were once people, who earned God status. So ordinary humans can ascend to godhood or immortality. Like Laozi who is now Lord Lao and is seen as almost an incarnation of the Dao itself. So, which of these deities are the most important in Daoist lives? Well the top Gods are probably, the Three Pure Ones (one of which is the deified Lao Tzu), the Jade Emperor, and the Eight Immortals. You may be imagining that they get the most attention, but actually no. Think of it like this: Whenever you need something from the government like getting a driver’s licence you don’t call the Prime Minister. Instead, you call the relevant government department for your particular problem. The Celestial Government works the same way. If you're having a problem with demons you'll do an offering to this guy, if you're having marriage problems then you'll be looking for this fella to help out, and if you want help in an exam this nerd would be your best bet. So those are the basics of Daoism. You might still be confused, and you should be. This is a very complicated religion and is inherently difficult to understand. Remember "The Dao that can be told of is not the eternal Dao ". This video isn't even close to covering everything. It would take much longer than 20 minutes to explain a religion.
